    11. Hibernate

    The previous chapter demonstrated how a Kotlin application interacts with a database through a JDBC driver: a connection is opened, SQL commands are executed, the result rows are read column by column, and they are copied into objects. This process of copying—from rows to objects and from objects to the [INSERT], [UPDATE], and [DELETE] commands—is repetitive. It can be automated using a tool: an “Object-Relational Mapper” (ORM). This chapter introduces the most widely used ORM in the Java world, Hibernate, and the standard it implements, Jakarta Persistence. Kotlin does not have its own ORM of the same caliber: it directly uses those from the Java platform—Hibernate foremost among them—just as it uses ORMs. You only need to know a few rules to write Kotlin entities that work with Hibernate: this chapter introduces them as we go along.

    The chapter revisits the sample code from the articles in Chapter 10 and concludes with version 7 of the tax calculation application, whose [dao] layer uses Hibernate.

    11.1. What is a ORM?

    11.1.1. Objects and Tables

    A Kotlin application works with objects: an item has a name, a price, and a stock level; an order has a customer and a list of line items, each of which refers to an item. A relational database stores this same information in tables: one row in the [articles] table per item, one row in the [commandes] table per order, with the relationships between rows expressed by foreign keys. The two worlds do not quite align:

    • an object directly references other objects ([commande.client]); a row contains the primary key value of another row ([client_id]);
    • an object can contain a collection ([commande.lignes]); a table contains only single values; the collection is represented by the rows of another table that point to the order;
    • the Kotlin types ([String], [BigDecimal], [LocalDate], [Boolean]) and the SQL types ([varchar(30)], [decimal(10,2)], [date], [bit]) are not the same;
    • objects are queried using Kotlin (the [filter], [map]... operations on collections) and tables are queried using SQL.

    A ORM bridges the two worlds. We define the correspondence between classes and tables (the model, or “mapping”) once and for all; it then takes care of:

    • translating queries written in an object-oriented language (HQL) or constructed using code (API Criteria) into SQL and [SELECT] commands ;
    • create objects from the read lines (this is called materialization);
    • to store the read objects and detect those that have been modified, added, or deleted;
    • to generate the [INSERT], [UPDATE], and [DELETE] commands that reflect these changes in the database;
    • and, if necessary, to create and update the database schema (tables, columns, indexes) based on the classes.

    The architecture of an application that uses Hibernate with MySQL is as follows:

    • [1]: the application. Its [dao] layer no longer communicates directly with the JDBC driver but with Hibernate, through a [Session] object and HQL queries;
    • [2]: Hibernate, independent of SGBD: model, query translation, change tracking, schema generation;
    • [3]: the dialect specific to SGBD (here, [MySQLDialect]): it knows the SQL syntax of SGBD, its column types, and its functions. The dialects of the main SGBDs are part of Hibernate itself: nothing needs to be added to the project;
    • [4]: the JDBC driver for SGBD, the one discussed in Chapter 10 (MySQL Connector/J): Hibernate does not replace JDBC; it uses it;
    • [5]: the SGBD.

    Whether the application is written in Java or Kotlin does not change this pattern: Hibernate is a Java library that Kotlin code calls just like any other Java library (Chapter 5), and the compiled Kotlin classes are, to Hibernate, Java classes just like any others.

    11.1.2. Jakarta Persistence and Hibernate

    Hibernate was created in 2001 by Gavin King in response to the cumbersomeness of the “entity beans” in the Java platform EE of that time. Its success was such that its ideas were incorporated into a standard, JPA (Java Persistence API), released in 2006 with Java EE 5. When Java EE was transferred to the Eclipse Foundation and renamed Jakarta EE, JPA became Jakarta Persistence, and its packages changed from [javax.persistence] to [jakarta.persistence] (version 3.0, 2020). The current version is Jakarta Persistence 3.2 (2024).

    Jakarta Persistence is a specification: a set of interfaces ([EntityManagerFactory], [EntityManager]...), annotations ([@Entity], [@Id], [@Column]...), and a query language, JPQL. It is implemented by several products: Hibernate ORM (the most widely used, used in Spring Boot and Quarkus), EclipseLink (the reference implementation)... This course uses Hibernate ORM 7.4.5, which implements Jakarta Persistence 3.2.

    Hibernate offers two ways to use it:

    • exclusively through the standard interfaces: in this case, the code depends only on [jakarta.persistence], and it would, in principle, be possible to switch implementations;
    • through its own (“native”) API, which is more feature-rich and whose interfaces extend those of the standard: a [SessionFactory] is a [EntityManagerFactory], and a [Session] is a [EntityManager].

    We use Hibernate’s own API, as recommended in its documentation: It provides all the standard methods ([persist], [find], [merge], [remove]...) as well as Hibernate’s extensions. The annotations, however, are always those defined by the standard. The following table shows the correspondences:

    Jakarta Persistence
    Hibernate
    Role
    [EntityManagerFactory]
    [SessionFactory]
    Hibernate configuration for a database: a heavy object, created once, shared by the entire application
    [EntityManager]
    [Session]
    A database session: a lightweight, short-lived object
    [EntityTransaction]
    [Transaction]
    a transaction
    JPQL
    HQL
    the query language; HQL is a superset of JPQL
    [CriteriaBuilder]
    [HibernateCriteriaBuilder]
    query construction via code

    In the Kotlin ecosystem, you’ll also encounter data access libraries of a different nature, such as Exposed (from JetBrains), which allows you to write SQL queries using a dedicated Kotlin language. These are lighter than a full ORM; Hibernate remains the standard for Spring applications, in both Java and Kotlin, and that is what we are studying.

    11.1.3. Libraries

    The libraries used in this chapter are as follows (they are summarized in the appendix on dependencies):

    Gradle Dependency
    Role
    [org.hibernate.orm:hibernate-core] 7.4.5.Final
    Hibernate itself; it includes the API from Jakarta Persistence 3.2 ([jakarta.persistence-api]) and its own dependencies (Byte Buddy for class generation, ANTLR for query analysis, JBoss Logging for logging, etc.)
    [com.mysql:mysql-connector-j] 9.7.0
    the JDBC driver for MySQL, the one from Chapter 10
    [ch.qos.logback:logback-classic] 1.5.38
    Logback, which will receive the Hibernate log

    Hibernate writes its log (executed SQL commands, warnings, etc.) through JBoss Logging, a small library that simply forwards messages to the logging system it finds in the classpath: Log4j 2, or Logback (via SLF4J), or, failing that, the one from JDK or [java.util.logging]. Without configuration, the latter displays each message on two lines, in red in most consoles, which makes the program output difficult to read. We therefore add Logback to our projects and configure it using a [logback.xml] file.

    In addition to these libraries, there are two Kotlin compiler plugins that adapt Kotlin classes to Hibernate’s requirements: [kotlin("plugin.jpa")] and [kotlin("plugin.allopen")]. We’ll see why they’re necessary when we look at the first entity.

    11.1.4. Code-First or Database-First

    The model (the mapping between classes and tables) can be built in two ways:

    • code-first: you write the Kotlin classes, and Hibernate infers the database schema from them, which it can then create on its own. This is the approach taken in this chapter;
    • database-first: the database already exists, and the classes are generated from its schema using Hibernate’s reverse-engineering tools (Hibernate Tools) or those provided by development environments (IntelliJ IDEA can generate entities from database tables in both Java and Kotlin). This is the approach used for applications that need to work with an existing database. The generated code is similar to what we would write by hand.

    11.2.2. The entity [Article]

    A class whose objects are stored in a table is called an entity. Our first entity is a store item, as in the table [articles] from Chapter 10:

    package premier

import jakarta.persistence.Entity
import jakarta.persistence.GeneratedValue
import jakarta.persistence.GenerationType
import jakarta.persistence.Id
import java.math.BigDecimal

// a store item: a regular Kotlin class, plus a few annotations
@Entity
class Article(
     // the table columns, declared as properties of the primary constructor
    var nom: String,
    var prix: BigDecimal,
    var stockActuel: Int,
    var stockMinimum: Int,
) {
     // the primary key, generated by SGBD: null until the item is saved
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    var id: Int? = null

     // display
    override fun toString() = "[%d, %s, %.2f, %d, %d]".format(id, nom, prix, stockActuel, stockMinimum)
}
    • Line 10: The annotation [@Entity] (package [jakarta.persistence]) makes the class an entity. This is a regular Kotlin class that does not extend any Hibernate class; it is referred to as a POJO (“Plain Old Java Object”);
    • lines 13–16: the properties declared in the primary constructor (Chapter 4). These are [var]: Hibernate must be able to modify their values, and so must the application (to change a price or inventory level). Each property becomes a column with the same name;
    • lines 19–21: the primary key is designated by the [@Id] annotation. There is no naming convention: the annotation is required. [@GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)] indicates that its values will be generated by SGBD (the [AUTO_INCREMENT] column of MySQL). The identifier is not a constructor parameter: it will be provided by SGBD. Its type is [Int?], and its initial value is [null], which means “not yet recorded in the database.” The type [Int?] is compiled into [java.lang.Integer], and the type [Int] into [int] (Chapter 3);
    • line 24: a convenient display of the item. The format [%.2f] displays the price with two decimal places, in accordance with common cultural conventions (a comma in France).

    Where do annotations go? In bytecode, a Kotlin property corresponds to several Java elements: a private field, an accessor ([getX]), a modifier ([setX]), and, in this case, a constructor parameter. An annotation placed before a property, without further specification, is positioned by Kotlin 2.4 based on the targets it accepts: on the constructor parameter if it is a constructor property and if the annotation allows it, and additionally on the Kotlin property itself if the annotation allows it; otherwise, on the field. Jakarta Persistence annotations ([@Id], [@Column]...) do not apply to Kotlin parameters or properties, but only to Java fields and methods: they are therefore placed on the field. This is exactly what we want: since the [@Id] annotation is on a field, Hibernate accesses the fields directly (it reads and writes them via reflection, even if they are private). You can verify this using the [javap] tool from JDK, which displays the contents of a [.class] file. You can also specify the target of an annotation using a prefix: [@field:Column(length = 30)] places it on the field, [@get:Transient] on the accessor.

    Jakarta Persistence requires two things that Kotlin classes do not provide out of the box:

    • a parameterless constructor, which Hibernate uses to create objects read from the database (it then populates their fields). Our class has only one constructor, with four parameters. In Java, you manually add a protected parameterless constructor. In Kotlin, it is the compiler plugin [no-arg], configured for JPA ([kotlin("plugin.jpa")]), that adds it to any class annotated with [@Entity], [@Embeddable], or [@MappedSuperclass]. This constructor exists in the bytecode, where Hibernate finds it through reflection, but it is not visible from the Kotlin code: [Article()] remains a compilation error (“[no value passed for parameter 'nom'.]”). Note that it does not execute property initializations: a property declared as [var x = "a"] is set to [null] in an object created by Hibernate, as long as Hibernate has not assigned a value to it (the [noArg { invokeInitializers = true }] option in the build file changes this behavior). This is not a problem for properties stored in the database, since Hibernate assigns them the value that was read;
    • non-final classes and methods. To implement lazy loading (which we’ll cover when discussing relationships), Hibernate creates proxies at runtime: classes derived from the entities, whose methods load the object from the database on the first call. For this to work, the class and its methods must be overridable. In Java, this is the default behavior; in Kotlin, classes and their members are final by default (Chapter 4). The [all-open] ([kotlin("plugin.allopen")]) plugin, configured by the [allOpen] block in the build file, makes classes bearing one of the listed annotations—as well as their properties and methods—non-final ([open]). The [plugin.spring] plugin from Chapter 6 is the same plugin, configured for Spring annotations.

    With these two plugins, the entity is written as a regular Kotlin class. Without them, you would have to write [open class Article(...)], declare [open] for each property, and add a secondary constructor with no parameters: we’ll do this for a class without annotations in the following example.

    Why not use a data class ([data class], Chapter 4)? It would seem ideal for representing a table row. However, this is a bad idea for an entity, for several reasons:

    • The generated methods [equals] and [hashCode] compare all properties of the primary constructor, which are modifiable. The hash code of an entity therefore changes as soon as its price is modified: an item stored in a [HashSet] or serving as the key of a [HashMap] becomes untraceable. Hibernate itself stores the elements of relationship collections ([Set]) using these methods;
    • two objects representing two different rows (with two different identifiers) but with the same values would be considered equal, whereas an item read from the database and then modified would no longer be equal to itself when read again;
    • the generated [toString] method displays all properties: with relationships, it iterates through the linked objects, which can cause them to be loaded from the database (unexpected SQL queries), an exception if the session is closed, or even an infinite recursion between two entities that reference each other;
    • The method [copy] creates a new object with the same identifier, which is unknown to the session: this results in two objects for the same row, which can lead to confusion;
    • A data class cannot be declared as open ([open]) by the programmer. The [all-open] plugin opens it anyway, which allows proxies to be created (we verified this using the [javap] tool), but it does not correct any of the previous issues.

    An entity is therefore an ordinary class: its identity is that of the table row, not the value of its properties. As in Java, it retains the [equals]/[hashCode] inherited from [Any] (object identity), which is fine as long as you do not mix objects from different sessions. Data classes remain very useful with Hibernate for query results that are not entities (projections), as we will see. This is the same rule as in Java, where an entity cannot be a record.

    One final note: Hibernate does not recognize Kotlin’s nullable types. The fact that the property [nom] is of type [String] (non-nullable) does not tell Hibernate that the column is required; only the annotation [@Column(nullable = false)] tells it that, as we’ll see in the results.

    11.2.3. [SessionFactory] and [Session]

    The program uses three Hibernate objects:

    • the [SessionFactory] represents Hibernate configured for a database: the list of entities, the database, and the options. Its creation is resource-intensive (Hibernate analyzes the entities, connects to the server to determine its version, and prepares the SQL for common operations): only one is created per database and per application, at startup. It is thread-safe: all application threads can use it;
    • the [Session] represents a working session with the database. It obtains a connection when needed, stores the entities it has read or saved, and knows how to commit their changes to the database. It is a lightweight, short-lived object that is not thread-safe: one is opened for each unit of work and then closed;
    • [Transaction]: With Hibernate, all writes to the database occur within an explicit transaction, opened by [session.beginTransaction()] and closed by [commit] (commit) or [rollback] (rollback).

    [SessionFactory] and [Session] implement the [AutoCloseable] interface: they are used with the Kotlin function [use] (Chapter 3), which closes them at the end of the block, whether it terminates normally or with an exception (the equivalent of the [try] statement with Java resources).

    package premier

import org.hibernate.jpa.HibernatePersistenceConfiguration
import java.math.BigDecimal

fun main() {
     // the SessionFactory: Hibernate configured for the [hbpremier] database
    HibernatePersistenceConfiguration("premier")
         // the entities
        .managedClass(Article::class.java)
         // the database; MySQL creates it if it does not exist
        .jdbcUrl("jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/hbpremier?createDatabaseIfNotExist=true")
        .jdbcCredentials("root", "")
         // display of SQL orders, formatted, without colors
        .showSql(true, true, false)
        .createEntityManagerFactory().use { sessionFactory ->

             // the tables are deleted and then recreated from the entities
            sessionFactory.schemaManager.drop(false)
            sessionFactory.schemaManager.create(false)

             // Adds three items in a single transaction
            sessionFactory.openSession().use { session ->
                val transaction = session.beginTransaction()
                println("--- persist")
                session.persist(Article("vélo", BigDecimal(500), 10, 5))
                session.persist(Article("pompe", BigDecimal(10), 10, 2))
                session.persist(Article("arc", BigDecimal(600), 4, 1))
                println("--- commit")
                transaction.commit()
            }

             // Reading the table with a new session
            println("--- lecture des articles")
            sessionFactory.openSession().use { session ->
                val articles: List<Article> = session
                    .createSelectionQuery("from Article order by nom", Article::class.java)
                    .resultList
                articles.forEach { println(it) }
            }
        }
}
    • lines 8–16: creation of the [SessionFactory]. There are several ways to configure Hibernate (we’ll discuss them later); we’re using the [HibernatePersistenceConfiguration] class from Hibernate 7, an enhanced version of the [PersistenceConfiguration] class introduced with Jakarta Persistence 3.2, which allows you to configure everything via code. Its parameter is the name of the persistence unit—a freely chosen name that appears in Hibernate messages. Each method returns the configuration itself, allowing calls to be chained together;
    • line 10: the list of entities. [Article::class.java] is the Java object [Class] (the Kotlin class [KClass] is not suitable: Hibernate is a Java library);
    • Lines 12–13: the URL JDBC from the [hbpremier] database, in the same format as in Chapter 10, and the user ([root], with no password in Laragon). The parameter [createDatabaseIfNotExist=true] of URL is an option of the driver MySQL: it creates the database if it does not exist;
    • Line 15: [showSql(true, true, false)] instructs Hibernate to print each SQL command it executes to the console, formatted across multiple lines (second parameter), without colors (third parameter). Looking at the SQL sent to the server is the best way to understand what Hibernate does: we’ll do this in all the examples;
    • Line 16: [createEntityManagerFactory] constructs [SessionFactory] (the method name follows the standard; the returned type is Hibernate’s). The function [use] will close it at the end of the program; within the block, it is called [sessionFactory];
    • Lines 19–20: The [SchemaManager] object of [SessionFactory] (Jakarta Persistence 3.2) manages the entity tables: [drop(false)] deletes them if they exist, while [create(false)] creates them (the parameter [false] specifies that the database itself should not be deleted or created). This is convenient for examples and tests; a real-world application manages its database differently, as we will see. Kotlin presents the Java method [getSchemaManager()] as a property, [schemaManager] (Chapter 4);
    • line 23: [openSession()] opens a session, which is closed at the end of the [use] block;
    • line 24: the start of a transaction;
    • lines 26–28: [persist] adds three new items to the session: they will be stored in the database. No value is specified for the identifier; it will be generated by SGBD;
    • line 30: [commit] commits the transaction. Prior to this, the session sends the SQL commands to the server, which are still necessary to save the changes it has stored: this is referred to as “flushing” the session to the database;
    • lines 36–38: a query written in HQL, Hibernate’s query language: the articles in alphabetical order by name. It refers to the entity [Article] and its property [nom], not to the table. The second parameter of [createSelectionQuery] is the result type: the property [resultList] (the Java method [getResultList]) returns a [List<Article>];
    • Line 39: Displaying the items.

    If an exception were to occur between [beginTransaction] and [commit], the transaction would neither be committed nor explicitly rolled back by our code: we’ll see later a safer way to write a transaction using a higher-order function.

    Comments:

    • Lines 2–17: Hibernate informational messages: the name of the persistence unit, the Hibernate version, and database characteristics (URL, driver, selected dialect, server version, transaction isolation level, connection pool size). Hibernate queried the server to select the [MySQLDialect] dialect appropriate for its version;
    • line 4: a warning. Hibernate manages its own small connection pool, which is not intended for a production application. We’ll see, with Spring, how to provide it with the HikariCP pool from Chapter 10; for our examples, the built-in pool is sufficient;
    • Lines 18–28: Deleting and then creating the table [Article] based on the entity: the table name is the same as the entity’s name, the columns are named after the properties, and the column [id] is the primary key, with a generated value ([auto_increment]). The columns for properties of type [Int] are [not null]: compiled into [int]; a [Int] cannot equal [null]. Properties of type [String] and [BigDecimal] accept the value [NULL], even though these types are non-nullable in Kotlin: for Hibernate, these are Java references ([java.lang.String], [java.math.BigDecimal]), which can be set to [null];
    • note the default types: [varchar(255)] for a string, and [decimal(38,2)] for a [BigDecimal] (38 digits, including 2 decimal places). These are rarely the ones you want: the following paragraph shows how to specify them;
    • Lines 29–51: The three configured [INSERT] commands were executed as soon as [persist] was called, before [commit]. This is a consequence of the key being generated by SGBD ([IDENTITY]): the session must know an entity’s identifier as soon as it takes over that entity, and to obtain it, it must execute the insertion (the JDBC driver returns the generated key; see Chapter 10). With other generation methods, insertions are deferred until the session is synchronized. The parameter values ([?]) are not displayed: we will see how to make them appear;
    • lines 53–63: the query HQL [from Article order by nom] was translated into a statement [SELECT ... ORDER BY]. Hibernate assigned the alias [a1_0] to the table and created a [Article] object for each row read (lines 64–66), using the parameterless constructor added by the [no-arg] plugin.

    We did not write any SQL statements or any column-reading code: that is the whole point of a ORM. We can also see that this does not eliminate the need to understand SQL: to determine whether the generated SQL is correct and effective, you need to know how to read it.

    11.3. The Model

    Hibernate builds its model from entities in three steps:

    • First, it applies its default rules: anything that isn’t specified is assigned a reasonable value (this is known as “configuration by exception”);
    • it then supplements or corrects these values using the annotations placed on the entities;
    • finally, it applies the mapping files XML ([orm.xml]), which can fully describe a class without annotations or modify what its annotations specify.

    11.3.1. Default Rules

    We saw the essentials of this in the first example:

    • an entity carries the annotation [@Entity] and has an identifier designated by [@Id]; both of these annotations are required;
    • the placement of the [@Id] annotation determines the access mode: when placed on a field, Hibernate reads and writes the fields directly; When placed on a getter or setter ([getId]), access goes through the getters and setters ([getX]/[setX]). Access via fields is the most common: it allows the class to have whatever methods it wants. In Kotlin, an annotation placed before a property is applied to the field (as we’ve seen): this provides access via fields without any explicit specification. For access via getters and setters, you would need to write [@get:Id];
    • any property that has a backing field is stored in a column, unless it bears the Jakarta Persistence annotation [@Transient] or the annotation [@kotlin.jvm.Transient] (which adds the Java modifier [transient] to the field); a calculated property, whose custom accessor does not use [field] (Chapter 4), has no field: it is never stored;
    • the table name is the entity name (the simple class name), and the column name is the property name. These names then go through a naming strategy: Hibernate’s strategy keeps the names as-is, while another strategy—which we’ll try below—converts them to “snake case” ([stockActuel] becomes [stock_actuel]). Spring Boot uses the latter by default;
    • a column of a type compiled to a primitive type (non-nullable [Int], [Double], [Boolean]) becomes [NOT NULL]; a column of a type compiled to a reference ([Int?], [String], [BigDecimal], [LocalDate], whether nullable or not for Kotlin) accepts the value [NULL]. To make a column of a property of type [String] mandatory, you must therefore use the annotation [@Column(nullable = false)], even though the Kotlin type already prohibits the value [null];
    • The SQL types are selected based on the dialect. With MySQL: [integer] for [Int], [bigint] for [Long], [bit] for [Boolean], [varchar(255)] for [String], [decimal(38,2)] for [BigDecimal], [date] for [LocalDate], [datetime(6)] (to the microsecond) for [LocalDateTime]. An enumeration ([enum class]) is registered by default by its sequence number (see Chapter 3); the annotation [@Enumerated(EnumType.STRING)] registers it by its name, which is more reliable;
    • a property that refers to another entity, or to a collection of entities, defines a relationship (we will discuss this later).

Its build file is that of [premier], with the Logback dependency replaced by a dependency on the [outils] library described below (which provides Logback and its configuration).     package modele

import jakarta.persistence.Column
import jakarta.persistence.Entity
import jakarta.persistence.GeneratedValue
import jakarta.persistence.GenerationType
import jakarta.persistence.Id
import jakarta.persistence.Table
import jakarta.persistence.Transient
import java.math.BigDecimal
import java.time.LocalDate

// An entity configured using annotations
@Entity
@Table(name = "produits")
class Produit(
     // Required string of up to 50 characters
    @Column(nullable = false, length = 50)
    var nom: String,

     // column name and type (SQL) are required
    @Column(name = "prix_ht", nullable = false, precision = 10, scale = 2)
    var prixHT: BigDecimal,

     // Optional string (column NULL) of up to 200 characters
    @Column(length = 200)
    var description: String? = null,

     // an optional date: a nullable type
    var dateRetrait: LocalDate? = null,
) {
     // the primary key: @Id, regardless of its name
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    var code: Int? = null

     // a property without a column
    @Transient
    var selectionne = false

     // a computed property has no field: it is never saved
    val prixTTC: BigDecimal
        get() = prixHT * BigDecimal("1.2")
}
    • lines 3–9: the Jakarta Persistence annotations. The explicit import of [jakarta.persistence.Transient] takes precedence over the annotation [kotlin.jvm.Transient]—which has the same name—that Kotlin imports by default;
    • line 15: [@Table] specifies the table name;
    • lines 18–19: [@Column] specifies the column; [nullable = false] makes it required ([NOT NULL]); [length = 50] sets its length ([varchar(50)]);
    • lines 22–23: [@Column] also specifies the column name ([prix_ht]) and, for a decimal number, its precision (the total number of digits) and its scale (the number of digits after the decimal point): [decimal(10,2)];
    • lines 26–27: an optional description of up to 200 characters: the column will accept the value [NULL]. The property is of type [String?], with the default value [null]: the Kotlin type matches the column. It is good practice to match the property’s nullable or non-nullable type with the column’s optional or required nature, even though Hibernate only reads the annotation;
    • line 30: an optional date. The type [LocalDate] (Chapter 5) represents a date without a time: it is associated with the types SQL and [date];
    • lines 32–35: the primary key, designated by [@Id] regardless of its name;
    • lines 38–39: [@Transient] excludes a property from the model: in this case, information useful to the user interface that does not belong in the database;
    • lines 42–43: a computed property. Its accessor does not use a field: there is nothing to save, and Hibernate, which accesses the fields, ignores it. The operator [*] between two [BigDecimal] is the function [times] that the Kotlin standard library adds to [BigDecimal] (Chapter 4, Operator Overloading): we write [prixHT * BigDecimal("1.2")] instead of Java’s [prixHT.multiply(new BigDecimal("1.2"))].

    package modele

import java.time.LocalDateTime

// a class with no annotations: its mapping is described by the file [fournisseur.orm.xml]
// The plugins [jpa] and [allopen] do not recognize it: it is declared as [open]
// and has its own parameterless constructor
open class Fournisseur(
    private var raisonSociale: String,
    private var telephone: String?,
) {
    private var numero: Int? = null
    private var dateCreation: LocalDateTime? = null

     // the parameterless constructor required by Hibernate
    protected constructor() : this("", null)
}
    • Line 8: Since the class is not annotated with [@Entity], the [no-arg] and [all-open] plugins do not recognize it. So we declare it ourselves as [open], so that Hibernate can derive proxies from it;
    • lines 9–13: private properties: Kotlin generates neither accessors nor mutators for them, only a private field, which Hibernate will read from and write to. This is the exact equivalent of private fields in a Java class;
    • Line 16: The parameterless constructor required by Hibernate, written by hand: a secondary constructor that calls the primary constructor (Chapter 4) with arbitrary values, which Hibernate will replace with those read from the database. It is protected: the application code will not use it.

    <?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!-- the mapping of the class [Fournisseur] to its table, described in XML (Jakarta Persistence 3.2) -->
<entity-mappings xmlns="https://jakarta.ee/xml/ns/persistence/orm"
                 xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
                 xsi:schemaLocation="https://jakarta.ee/xml/ns/persistence/orm
                                     https://jakarta.ee/xml/ns/persistence/orm/orm_3_2.xsd"
                 version="3.2">
    <entity class="modele.Fournisseur" access="FIELD">
        <table name="fournisseurs">
             <!-- a unique index: two suppliers cannot have the same company name -->
            <index name="ix_fournisseurs_raison_sociale" column-list="raisonSociale" unique="true"/>
        </table>
        <attributes>
            <id name="numero">
                <generated-value strategy="IDENTITY"/>
            </id>
            <basic name="raisonSociale">
                <column nullable="false" length="60"/>
            </basic>
            <basic name="telephone">
                <column name="tel" length="20"/>
            </basic>
             <!-- a default value calculated by SGBD: Hibernate never writes to this column -->
            <basic name="dateCreation">
                <column nullable="false" insertable="false" updatable="false"
                        column-definition="datetime(6) default current_timestamp(6)"/>
            </basic>
        </attributes>
    </entity>
</entity-mappings>
    • lines 3–7: the XML schema for Jakarta Persistence 3.2 mapping files;
    • line 8: the described class, with access via fields;
    • lines 9–12: the table, and a unique index on the company name: no two suppliers can have the same one. The equivalent annotation is [@Table(name = "fournisseurs", indexes = [Index(...)])] (in Kotlin, an array passed as an annotation argument is written in square brackets);
    • lines 14–16: the identifier, generated by SGBD;
    • lines 17–18: a required column with a maximum of 60 characters;
    • lines 20–21: the property [telephone] is stored in the column [tel];
    • lines 24–26: the creation date has a default value, calculated by SGBD. The [column-definition] attribute provides the text SQL from the column definition, copied verbatim in the order [CREATE TABLE]; [insertable="false"] and [updatable="false"] indicate that Hibernate must never write to this column, which allows SGBD to use [current_timestamp(6)].

    Everything that annotations do can be done in XML. Annotations have the advantage of placing the configuration next to the property, and this is the most common approach; the XML file, on the other hand, keeps the classes independent of Jakarta Persistence and centralizes the configuration in a single location. The two approaches can be combined: the XML file takes precedence in case of a conflict. Jakarta Persistence does not support configuring the model via code, as other frameworks such as ORM (for example, Entity Framework in C# or Exposed in Kotlin) do.

    package modele

import jakarta.persistence.metamodel.SingularAttribute
import org.hibernate.boot.model.naming.PhysicalNamingStrategySnakeCaseImpl
import org.hibernate.cfg.AvailableSettings
import org.hibernate.jpa.HibernatePersistenceConfiguration
import java.io.StringWriter

fun main() {
     // The table creation script will be written to this object
    val script = StringWriter()
     // a SessionFactory that never connects to the server
    HibernatePersistenceConfiguration("modele")
         // An annotated entity and a mapping described in XML
        .managedClass(Produit::class.java)
        .mappingFile("META-INF/fournisseur.orm.xml")
         // no database: the SGBD and its version are provided for the SQL dialect
        .property(AvailableSettings.JAKARTA_HBM2DDL_DB_NAME, "MySQL")
        .property(AvailableSettings.JAKARTA_HBM2DDL_DB_MAJOR_VERSION, "8")
        .property(AvailableSettings.ALLOW_METADATA_ON_BOOT, false)
         // column names in “snake case”: raisonSociale -> raison_sociale
        .property(AvailableSettings.PHYSICAL_NAMING_STRATEGY,
            PhysicalNamingStrategySnakeCaseImpl::class.java.name)
         // the table creation script, without executing it
        .property(AvailableSettings.JAKARTA_HBM2DDL_SCRIPTS_ACTION, "create")
        .property(AvailableSettings.JAKARTA_HBM2DDL_SCRIPTS_CREATE_TARGET, script)
        .property(AvailableSettings.HBM2DDL_DELIMITER, ";")
        .property(AvailableSettings.FORMAT_SQL, true)
        .createEntityManagerFactory().use { sessionFactory ->

             // the model built by Hibernate: entities and attributes (API Jakarta Persistence)
            for (entite in sessionFactory.metamodel.entities) {
                println("entité ${entite.name} (${entite.javaType.name})")
                for (attribut in entite.attributes) {
                    val id = attribut is SingularAttribute<*, *> && attribut.isId
                    println("  %-14s %s%s".format(attribut.name, attribut.javaType.simpleName,
                        if (id) " (identifiant)" else ""))
                }
            }
        }
     // the table creation script, without removing 4 spaces from its lines
    println("--- script de création")
    script.toString().trim().lines()
        .map { it.removePrefix("    ") }
        .forEach { println(it.trimEnd()) }
}
    • line 11: a [StringWriter] (package [java.io]), a write stream to a string in memory, will receive the script SQL;
    • lines 15–16: the annotated entity is declared by [managedClass], and the file XML by [mappingFile];
    • lines 18–20: The database will never exist: this [SessionFactory] is used solely to examine the model. Therefore, there is no URL or JDBC. To select the SQL dialect without querying the server, Hibernate needs the name of the SGBD and its version; the [ALLOW_METADATA_ON_BOOT] property ([hibernate.boot.allow_jdbc_metadata_access]) prevents it from connecting at startup. The names of the configuration properties are constants in the [AvailableSettings] interface;
    • line 22: the “snake case” naming convention, denoted by the name of its class ([::class.java.name]);
    • lines 25–28: Hibernate will write the table creation script (["create"]) to the [script] object without executing it; the commands are terminated by a semicolon and formatted across multiple lines;
    • line 32: the property [metamodel] (the [getMetamodel] method from Jakarta Persistence) provides access to the model: its entities ([EntityType]) and, for each one, its attributes ([Attribute]);
    • Lines 33–37: For each entity, its name and class; for each attribute, its name, Java type, and whether it is the identifier. On line 35, the [attribut is SingularAttribute<*, *>] test is followed by a smart type conversion (Chapter 4): in the continuation of the expression [&&], [attribut] is a [SingularAttribute], from which the property [isId] can be read. The [<*, *>] projection replaces Java’s [<?, ?>];
    • Lines 42–45: The script as displayed, without the four spaces that Hibernate adds to its lines ([removePrefix] removes the prefix only if it is present).

    11.3.3. Generated identifiers

    The annotation [@GeneratedValue] indicates that the identifier value is generated. Its parameter [strategy] specifies how:

    Strategy
    Identifier Generation
    [IDENTITY]
    by SGBD, when inserting the row (column [AUTO_INCREMENT] of MySQL, [IDENTITY] of SQL Server, and PostgreSQL)
    [SEQUENCE]
    by a sequence from SGBD (PostgreSQL, Oracle), which Hibernate queries before insertion
    [TABLE]
    by a counter table managed by Hibernate
    [UUID]
    by Hibernate: a random universal identifier, such as [java.util.UUID]
    [AUTO] (by default)
    Hibernate chooses; with MySQL, which has no sequences, it simulates them using a table named [<table>_SEQ]

    With MySQL, we always use [IDENTITY], which corresponds to the natural behavior of the [AUTO_INCREMENT] column. We’ve seen the result of this: the [INSERT] command is executed as soon as [persist] is called, and Hibernate cannot group multiple inserts into a batch (we’ll discuss batches later). The [SEQUENCE] strategy, which allows you to know the ID before the insertion, is preferred for SGBD methods that use sequences.

    In Kotlin, the generated identifier should preferably be declared as [var id: Int? = null]: the value [null] clearly indicates “not yet registered.” We also encounter [var id: Int = 0], where the value 0 serves this purpose; Hibernate accepts it (for an identifier of a primitive type, it treats 0 as the “not yet registered” value), but this convention is less readable.

    11.3.4. Optional Values and Columns [NULL]

    Whether a column is optional is therefore determined by the property’s type (compiled as a primitive type or a reference) and by the [nullable] attribute of [@Column]; in Kotlin, the property type also specifies whether the value may be missing ([String?]) or not ([String]). You must choose carefully and ensure that the two match: the rule expresses both a code constraint (“this value may be missing”) and a database constraint. A few notes:

    • [@Column(nullable = false)] represents the constraint [NOT NULL] from the schema created by Hibernate, and Hibernate also uses it before sending a command [INSERT] or [UPDATE]: if the field is [null], it does not send the command and throws a [PropertyValueException] error (“not-null property references a null or transient value”). This Hibernate check is disabled by default when Jakarta Validation (below) is present: validation then falls back to its annotations, or, failing that, to SGBD, which rejects the command. In Kotlin, this scenario is less common than in Java: the compiler prohibits assigning [null] to a property of type [String];
    • for a more comprehensive validation performed before any database access, we use Jakarta Validation ([hibernate-validator] library) and its annotations [@NotNull], [@Size(max = 30)], [@Positive]... When present in the classpath, Hibernate validates entities before saving them and uses these annotations to create the columns. In Kotlin, these annotations also accept parameters as targets: when applied to a constructor property, Kotlin 2.4 applies them to both the parameter and the field, which the validator reads. Earlier versions placed them only on the parameter: you had to specify the field target, [@field:Size(max = 30)], a form that is still encountered in many examples;
    • there is no need to use [Optional] (Chapter 4): Kotlin’s nullable type ([var description: String? = null]) directly indicates that a value is optional, and it is read using the operators [?.] and [?:] (Chapter 3): [produit.description ?: "(pas de description)"].

    11.4. The following examples: two common libraries

    The examples in the following paragraphs almost all use the [hbarticles] database and its [articles] table, populated with the six entries from Chapter 10. Rather than repeating the Hibernate entity and configuration in each subproject, we place them in a library—the [articles] subproject—on which the other subprojects depend. We also replace the SQL log from [showSql]—which is too verbose for our examples—with a more compact log, placed in a second library, the [outils] subproject.

    11.4.1. The compact SQL log

    Rather than writing directly to the console ([showSql]), Hibernate can forward its activity to the logging system (in this case, Logback), with each message category written to a different logger:

    Log
    Level
    Messages
    [org.hibernate.SQL]
    [DEBUG]
    SQL orders executed
    [org.hibernate.orm.jdbc.bind]
    [TRACE]
    the value of each parameter in an order SQL
    [org.hibernate.orm.resource.jdbc]
    [TRACE]
    including, among other things, the initiation, confirmation, and cancellation of transactions
    [org.hibernate.orm.jdbc.batch]
    [TRACE]
    execution of order batches SQL
    [org.hibernate.orm.jdbc.error]
    [WARN]
    Errors reported by SGBD

    A log only records messages of a level equal to or higher than its own. Therefore, you simply need to set the desired level for these logs in the [logback.xml] file to capture these messages. We process them through a layout class that makes them more compact:

    package outils

import ch.qos.logback.classic.Level
import ch.qos.logback.classic.Logger
import ch.qos.logback.classic.spi.ILoggingEvent
import ch.qos.logback.core.LayoutBase
import org.slf4j.LoggerFactory

// A compact log of SQL commands executed by Hibernate: a Logback layout
class JournalSql : LayoutBase<ILoggingEvent>() {

     // message layout: the text to be written is rendered ("": nothing is written)
    override fun doLayout(evenement: ILoggingEvent): String {
        val message = evenement.formattedMessage
        return when (evenement.loggerName) {
            SQL -> ordreSql(message)
            PARAMETRES -> parametre(message)
            TRANSACTIONS -> transaction(message)
            ERREURS -> erreur(message)
            LOTS -> lot(message)
            else -> ""
        }
    }

    companion object {
         // the Hibernate loggers used
        const val SQL = "org.hibernate.SQL"
        const val PARAMETRES = "org.hibernate.orm.jdbc.bind"
        const val TRANSACTIONS = "org.hibernate.orm.resource.jdbc"
        const val ERREURS = "org.hibernate.orm.jdbc.error"
        const val LOTS = "org.hibernate.orm.jdbc.batch"

         // the maximum length of a clause written on a single line
        private const val LARGEUR = 100

         // Execution of a batch of commands SQL: “Executing JDBC batch (3 / 3) - [...]”
        private val LOT = Regex("""Executing JDBC batch \((\d+) / \d+\).*""")

         // a parameter associated with an order SQL: “binding parameter (1:VARCHAR) <- [vélo]”
        private val PARAMETRE = Regex("""binding parameter \((\d+):\w+\) <- \[(.*)]""")

         // the SQL query formatted by Hibernate, made more compact: one line per clause (select, from...)
        private fun ordreSql(sql: String): String {
             // non-empty lines, without trailing spaces
            val lignes = sql.lines().map { it.trimEnd() }.filter { it.isNotBlank() }
             // the clauses: a top-level line (least indented) and the lines that follow it
            val retrait = lignes.minOfOrNull { retrait(it) } ?: 0
            val clauses = mutableListOf<MutableList<String>>()
            for (ligne in lignes) {
                if (clauses.isEmpty() || retrait(ligne) == retrait) clauses.add(mutableListOf())
                clauses.last().add(ligne.substring(retrait))
            }
             // each clause is written on a single line, if it is not too long
            var debut = ""
            return buildString {
                for (clause in clauses) {
                    val ligne = debut + clause.joinToString(" ") { it.trim() }
                    if (ligne == "insert" || ligne == "delete") {
                         // [insert into ...], [delete from ...]: a single line
                        debut = "$ligne "
                        continue
                    }
                    if (ligne.length <= LARGEUR) {
                        append("    SQL> ").append(ligne).append('\n')
                    } else {
                         // Clause too long: we keep the lines from Hibernate
                        clause.forEachIndexed { i, l ->
                            append("    SQL> ").append(if (i == 0) debut else "").append(l).append('\n')
                        }
                    }
                    debut = ""
                }
            }
        }

         // the number of spaces at the beginning of the line
        private fun retrait(ligne: String) = ligne.length - ligne.trimStart().length

         // the value of a parameter in the order SQL
        private fun parametre(message: String): String =
            PARAMETRE.matchEntire(message)
                ?.let { "    SQL> -- paramètre ${it.groupValues[1]} = ${it.groupValues[2]}\n" } ?: ""

         // start, commit, and rollback of transactions (other messages are ignored)
        private fun transaction(message: String): String = when {
            message.startsWith("HHH10003002") -> "    SQL> -- début de transaction\n"
            message.startsWith("HHH10003004") -> "    SQL> -- transaction validée (COMMIT)\n"
            message.startsWith("HHH10003006") -> "    SQL> -- transaction annulée (ROLLBACK)\n"
            else -> ""
        }

         // the error reported by SGBD (the line containing its error codes is ignored)
        private fun erreur(message: String): String =
            if (message.startsWith("HHH000247")) "" else "    SQL> -- échec : $message\n"

         // Execution of a batch of SQL orders (other messages are ignored)
        private fun lot(message: String): String =
            LOT.matchEntire(message)
                ?.let { "    SQL> -- exécution d'un lot de ${it.groupValues[1]} ordre(s)\n" } ?: ""

         // executes a non-logged action SQL and returns its result
        fun <T> sansJournal(action: () -> T): T {
            val journaux = listOf(SQL, PARAMETRES, TRANSACTIONS, ERREURS, LOTS)
                .map { LoggerFactory.getLogger(it) as Logger }
             // the current levels, restored at the end
            val niveaux: List<Level?> = journaux.map { it.level }
            journaux.forEach { it.level = Level.OFF }
            try {
                return action()
            } finally {
                journaux.zip(niveaux).forEach { (journal, niveau) -> journal.level = niveau }
            }
        }
    }
}
    • line 10: a Logback layout derives from the Java class [LayoutBase<ILoggingEvent>] (note the parentheses: the call to the parent class’s constructor, Chapter 4); its method [doLayout] (lines 13–21) receives each message (a [ILoggingEvent]) and returns the text to be written. Logback creates the object itself, via reflection, based on the class name: it requires a parameterless constructor, which is the class’s implicit primary constructor;
    • lines 15–21: the processing depends on the log that sent the message (a ***[when] on a channel, Chapter 3). The branches use the constants from ***[companion object];
    • line 25: the class’s “static” members are stored in its companion object (Chapter 4);
    • lines 27–31: the names of the Hibernate logs used and the public compilation constants ([const val]); other subprojects refer to them as [JournalSql.SQL]...;
    • lines 37–40: two regular expressions (Chapter 5), written as raw strings (["""..."""]), which avoids having to double the backslashes, as Java does (["\\((\\d+)..."]);
    • lines 43–71: the order SQL, as formatted by Hibernate ([format_sql]), spread across many lines, with one column per line. We make it more compact. Non-empty lines are grouped into clauses (lines 47–51): a clause begins with a top-level line ([select], [from], [where]...) and includes the indented lines that follow it. [minOfOrNull] specifies the smallest indentation, or [null] if there is no line, in which case it is replaced by 0 using the operator [?:]. Each clause is then written on a single line, preceded by [SQL>], if it does not exceed 100 characters (lines 63–64); otherwise, its lines are retained (lines 67–68). The clauses [insert] and [delete] are combined with the following one (lines 58–61). The text is constructed by [buildString] (Chapter 5), whose block has a [StringBuilder] as its receiver: [append] is called there without a prefix;
    • lines 80–82: the Hibernate message that returns the value of a parameter resembles [binding parameter (1:VARCHAR) <- [vélo]]. [matchEntire] returns a [MatchResult] if the entire message matches the regular expression, and [null] otherwise; [?.let] constructs the text from the captured groups (the parameter number and its value), and [?: ""] returns an empty string when there is no match;
    • Lines 85–89: Among the many messages in the [org.hibernate.orm.resource.jdbc] log, only those indicating the start, commit, and rollback of a transaction are retained. Each Hibernate message begins with a code ([HHH10003002]...) that uniquely identifies it. A [when] without arguments (Chapter 3) replaces Java’s [if] sequence;
    • lines 93–94: an error in SGBD. Hibernate writes this as two messages: one providing the error codes (which we ignore) and the other providing the error text;
    • lines 97–99: execution of a batch of SQL commands, which we will encounter at the end of the chapter;
    • lines 102–111: the function [sansJournal] executes a logless action SQL. This is a higher-order function (Chapter 7): its parameter is a function [() -> T], and it returns the result of the action (Java, which uses a [Runnable], does not allow this quite so easily). It uses Logback’s API: each log ([Logger]) has a level, which can be modified at runtime (the [level] property, which corresponds to the Java methods [getLevel]/[setLevel]). We set the five logs to level [OFF], execute the action, and then restore the original levels in a [finally] clause, so that they remain at those levels even if the action throws an exception. The original level may be [null] (a log that inherits its level from its parent), hence the type [List<Level?>]; [zip] associates each log with its original level, and the [(journal, niveau)] decomposition (Chapter 3) names the two elements of each pair;
    • line 104: [LoggerFactory] is the class of SLF4J that returns a log; Since Logback is the current implementation of SLF4J, the rendered object is a [ch.qos.logback.classic.Logger], as indicated by the type conversion [as Logger].

    <?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!-- Logback configuration for the examples in this chapter -->
<configuration>

     <!-- the compact log SQL: formatted by the class [outils.JournalSql] -->
    <appender name="SQL" class="ch.qos.logback.core.ConsoleAppender">
        <encoder class="ch.qos.logback.core.encoder.LayoutWrappingEncoder">
            <layout class="outils.JournalSql"/>
        </encoder>
    </appender>

     <!-- Other messages: level, log short name, text -->
    <appender name="CONSOLE" class="ch.qos.logback.core.ConsoleAppender">
        <encoder>
            <pattern>%-5level %logger{0} - %msg%n</pattern>
        </encoder>
    </appender>

     <!-- SQL commands (DEBUG), their parameters, transactions, batches (TRACE), and errors -->
    <logger name="org.hibernate.SQL" level="DEBUG" additivity="false">
        <appender-ref ref="SQL"/>
    </logger>
    <logger name="org.hibernate.orm.jdbc.bind" level="TRACE" additivity="false">
        <appender-ref ref="SQL"/>
    </logger>
    <logger name="org.hibernate.orm.resource.jdbc" level="TRACE" additivity="false">
        <appender-ref ref="SQL"/>
    </logger>
    <logger name="org.hibernate.orm.jdbc.batch" level="TRACE" additivity="false">
        <appender-ref ref="SQL"/>
    </logger>
    <logger name="org.hibernate.orm.jdbc.error" level="WARN" additivity="false">
        <appender-ref ref="SQL"/>
    </logger>

     <!-- Hibernate's built-in connection pool is sufficient for our examples: we ignore its warning -->
    <logger name="org.hibernate.orm.connections.pooling" level="ERROR"/>

     <!-- Deleting tables from an empty database causes harmless errors: we suppress them -->
    <logger name="org.hibernate.tool.schema" level="OFF"/>

     <!-- All other logs: warnings and errors only -->
    <root level="WARN">
        <appender-ref ref="CONSOLE"/>
    </root>
</configuration>
    • lines 6–10: An “appender” writes the messages, in this case to the console. It uses our layout, identified by its class name ([outils.JournalSql]);
    • lines 13–17: a second “appender” for the other messages: level, short log name, text;
    • Lines 20–34: The Hibernate logs from the previous table, along with their levels. Their messages are sent to the “appender” [SQL] and only to it ([additivity="false"]: they are not additionally forwarded to the root log);
    • line 37: the warning regarding Hibernate’s built-in connection pool is suppressed;
    • line 40: Hibernate deletes tables starting with their foreign keys; on an empty database, these deletions fail without consequence, but Hibernate logs this at length. These messages are suppressed;
    • lines 43–45: the other logs record only warnings and errors.

    package articles

import jakarta.persistence.Column
import jakarta.persistence.Entity
import jakarta.persistence.GeneratedValue
import jakarta.persistence.GenerationType
import jakarta.persistence.Id
import jakarta.persistence.Table
import jakarta.persistence.UniqueConstraint
import java.math.BigDecimal

// a store item, with annotations specifying its table
// a regular class (not a data class); the [jpa] plugin adds a constructor without
// parameters; the [allopen] plugin makes it open (non-final), along with its properties
@Entity
@Table(
    name = "articles",
    uniqueConstraints = [UniqueConstraint(name = "uk_articles_nom", columnNames = ["nom"])]
)
class Article(
     // item name: required, 30 characters or fewer, unique (see @Table)
    @Column(nullable = false, length = 30)
    var nom: String,
     // Price: 10 digits, including 2 decimal places
    @Column(nullable = false, precision = 10, scale = 2)
    var prix: BigDecimal,
     // current stock and minimum stock level below which restocking is required
    var stockActuel: Int,
    var stockMinimum: Int,
) {
     // primary key, generated by SGBD (AUTO_INCREMENT): null until the item is saved
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    var id: Int? = null
         // No modification by the application: the identifier is managed by Hibernate
        protected set

     // display
    override fun toString() = "[%d, %s, %.2f, %d, %d]".format(id, nom, prix, stockActuel, stockMinimum)
}
    • lines 13–14: a reminder of what the [jpa] and [allopen] plugins do for this class;
    • lines 16–18: the table is named [articles], as in Chapter 10. The parameter [uniqueConstraints] declares a uniqueness constraint, named [uk_articles_nom], on the column [nom]: two items cannot have the same name. Without an explicit name, Hibernate would generate an unreadable one ([UK3f8k...]), which would appear in error messages. Array-type annotation parameters are written in Kotlin within square brackets ([[UniqueConstraint(...)]], [["nom"]]); an annotation used as an argument for another annotation is written without [@];
    • lines 22–23: a required name of no more than 30 characters;
    • lines 25–26: a price in the format [decimal(10,2)];
    • lines 28–29: the two stock levels, of type [Int]: columns [NOT NULL];
    • lines 32–36: the identifier. The property modifier is declared as [protected]: the application can read the identifier but cannot change it, since it is managed by Hibernate (the Java class does not have a [setId] method, for the same reason). It could not be [private]: the property is public ([all-open]), and Kotlin prohibits a private modifier on a public property, which a derived class could redefine (“[private setters for open properties are prohibited.]”);
    • line 39: the same method [toString] as in the first example.

    The Java version of this class has nearly ninety lines, including the two constructors and about ten accessors ([getX]/[setX]); in Kotlin, the properties of the primary constructor and the two plugins serve this purpose.

    package articles

import org.hibernate.SessionFactory
import org.hibernate.cfg.AvailableSettings
import org.hibernate.jpa.HibernatePersistenceConfiguration
import outils.JournalSql
import java.math.BigDecimal

// the database [hbarticles]: Hibernate configuration and database initialization
// a [object]: a single instance, without a constructor (the Java utility class)
object BaseArticles {

     // the database; MySQL creates it if it does not exist (createDatabaseIfNotExist)
    const val URL = "jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/hbarticles?createDatabaseIfNotExist=true"
    const val UTILISATEUR = "root"
    const val MOT_DE_PASSE = ""

     // Hibernate configuration: entities, database, and log formatting (SQL)
    fun configuration(): HibernatePersistenceConfiguration =
        HibernatePersistenceConfiguration("articles")
            .managedClass(Article::class.java)
            .jdbcUrl(URL)
            .jdbcCredentials(UTILISATEUR, MOT_DE_PASSE)
            .property(AvailableSettings.FORMAT_SQL, true)

     // a SessionFactory for the [hbarticles] database, using the previous configuration
    fun creerSessionFactory(): SessionFactory = configuration().createEntityManagerFactory()

     // (re)creation of the table [articles] with its six records, without the log SQL
    fun initialiser(sessionFactory: SessionFactory) = JournalSql.sansJournal {
         // deletion and subsequent creation of the entity tables
        sessionFactory.schemaManager.drop(false)
        sessionFactory.schemaManager.create(false)
         // the six items, added in a single transaction
        sessionFactory.inTransaction { session ->
            session.persist(Article("vélo", BigDecimal(500), 10, 5))
            session.persist(Article("pompe", BigDecimal(10), 10, 2))
            session.persist(Article("arc", BigDecimal(600), 4, 1))
            session.persist(Article("flèches - lot de 6", BigDecimal(100), 12, 20))
            session.persist(Article("combinaison de plongée", BigDecimal(300), 8, 2))
            session.persist(Article("bouteilles d'oxygène", BigDecimal(120), 10, 5))
        }
    }
}
    • line 11: a [object] (Chapter 4): a singleton, created on first use. This is equivalent to a Java utility class (a [final] class with static members and a private constructor);
    • lines 14–16: the base URL and the user URL, which are public so that other subprojects can use them;
    • Lines 19–24: The Hibernate configuration. It is returned by a public function, which will allow an example to complete it before creating the [SessionFactory]. The [FORMAT_SQL] ([hibernate.format_sql]) property instructs Hibernate to format the SQL, which it then passes to the [org.hibernate.SQL] log: it is this formatted output that the [JournalSql] class then condenses;
    • line 27: the [SessionFactory] from the [hbarticles] base, a function whose body is an expression;
    • lines 30–41: a function that recreates the table [articles] with its six entries, without the log SQL: we do not want to see the SQL from this initialization in the example results. The block passed to [sansJournal] is a lambda written after the parentheses, which are omitted here (Chapter 7);
    • line 35: [sessionFactory.inTransaction { session -> ... }] opens a session, starts a transaction, executes the lambda by passing it the session, commits the transaction (or rolls it back if the lambda throws an exception), and closes the session. This is the shortest way to write a unit of work; we’ll use it often, along with its variants [inSession] (a session without a transaction), [fromTransaction], and [fromSession] (which return the result of the lambda). The parameter for these Java methods is a functional interface ([Consumer<Session>], [Function<Session, R>]): Kotlin directly accepts a lambda there (conversion SAM, Chapter 7);
    • lines 36–41: [BigDecimal(500)] calls the constructor of [BigDecimal], which takes an integer; it returns the same value as the Java method [BigDecimal.valueOf(500)].

    `java-library`
}

repositories {
    mavenCentral()
}

dependencies {
     // the compact SQL log (and Logback)
    api(project(":outils"))
     // Hibernate: [api], because library users work with SessionFactory, Session...
    api("org.hibernate.orm:hibernate-core:7.4.5.Final")
     // the JDBC driver for MySQL: useful only at runtime
    runtimeOnly("com.mysql:mysql-connector-j:9.7.0")
}

// Classes annotated in this way are opened by the [allopen] plugin
allOpen {
    annotation("jakarta.persistence.Entity")
    annotation("jakarta.persistence.MappedSuperclass")
    annotation("jakarta.persistence.Embeddable")

    11.4.3. Other Ways to Configure Hibernate

    We configure Hibernate programmatically using [HibernatePersistenceConfiguration]. There are other ways to do this, which can be found in applications and documentation:

    • a [META-INF/persistence.xml] file, the traditional approach used by Jakarta Persistence: it describes one or more persistence units (entity classes, connection properties, options), and the factory is created using [Persistence.createEntityManagerFactory("articles")];
    • a [hibernate.properties] (or [hibernate.cfg.xml]) file, specific to Hibernate, read by the [org.hibernate.cfg.Configuration] class: [Configuration().addAnnotatedClass(Article::class.java).buildSessionFactory()]. This is the approach used in older versions of Hibernate;
    • In a Spring Boot application, the properties [spring.datasource.*] and [spring.jpa.*] in the file [application.properties]: Spring Boot creates the factory itself.

    The properties are the same everywhere ([hibernate.format_sql], [jakarta.persistence.jdbc.url]...): only the way they are specified changes.

    11.5. Basic operations: add, read, update, delete

    11.5.1. The [crud] program

    The [crud] subproject demonstrates the four basic operations (CRUD: Create, Read, Update, Delete), as well as entity tracking via the session. To make this tracking visible, it uses a few internal Hibernate methods (its “SPI,” Service Provider Interface), intended for Hibernate extensions rather than applications: they are grouped in the utility functions at the end of the file, written as extension functions of [Session] (Chapter 4). Transactions are written using the session’s [inTransaction] method, a higher-order function: [session.inTransaction { ... }] starts a transaction, executes the block, and then commits the transaction or rolls it back if the block throws an exception. The code can no longer omit [commit] or [rollback] in the event of an error.

    package crud

import articles.Article
import articles.BaseArticles
import org.hibernate.Session
import org.hibernate.engine.spi.PersistenceContext
import org.hibernate.engine.spi.SessionImplementor
import java.math.BigDecimal

fun main() {
    BaseArticles.creerSessionFactory().use { sessionFactory ->
         // the [articles] table is recreated with its six entries
        BaseArticles.initialiser(sessionFactory)
        sessionFactory.openSession().use { session ->
             // 1 - search by primary key
            println("--- find(1)")
            val velo = session.find(Article::class.java, 1) ?: error("pas d'article n° 1")
            println(velo)
            println("--- find(1) une seconde fois")
            val velo2 = session.find(Article::class.java, 1)
            println("même objet : ${velo === velo2}")

             // 2 - Add an item in a transaction
            println("--- persist")
            val x = Article("x", BigDecimal(100), 10, 1)
            session.inTransaction {
                println("avant persist : état=${session.etat(x)}, id=${x.id}")
                session.persist(x)
                println("après persist : état=${session.etat(x)}, id=${x.id}")
            }

             // 3 - Update: simply modify the object
            println("--- modification du prix")
            session.inTransaction {
                x.prix *= BigDecimal("1.1")
                println("session modifiée : ${session.isDirty}, " +
                    "prix d'origine=${session.valeurOrigine(x, "prix")}, prix actuel=${x.prix}")
                println("--- commit")
            }
            println("après commit : session modifiée : ${session.isDirty}")

             // 4 - Deletion
            println("--- remove")
            session.inTransaction {
                session.remove(x)
                println("avant commit : état=${session.etat(x)}")
            }
            println("après commit : état=${session.etat(x)}")

             // 5 - an object detached, modified, and then merged with the session
            println("--- detach et merge")
            val arc = session.find(Article::class.java, 3) ?: error("pas d'article n° 3")
            session.detach(arc)
            println("après detach : état=${session.etat(arc)}")
            arc.prix = BigDecimal(550)
            session.inTransaction {
                val arcGere = session.merge(arc)
                println("merge : même objet=${arc === arcGere}, " +
                    "état de l'objet rendu=${session.etat(arcGere)}")
            }

             // 6 - Entities tracked by the session
            println("--- les entités suivies")
            velo.stockActuel--
            session.afficherEntitesSuivies()
        }
    }
}

// the session’s persistence context (Hibernate’s internal API): an extension property
private val Session.contexte: PersistenceContext
    get() = unwrap(SessionImplementor::class.java).persistenceContext

// the status of an item relative to the session (Hibernate’s internal API)
private fun Session.etat(article: Article): String = when {
     // an object tracked by the session: MANAGED, DELETED...
    contexte.isEntryFor(article) -> contexte.getEntry(article).status.name
     // an object unknown to the session: never saved (no ID) or detached
    article.id == null -> "TRANSIENT"
    else -> "DETACHED"
}

// the value of a property as read from the database (Hibernate's internal API)
private fun Session.valeurOrigine(entite: Any, propriete: String): Any? =
    contexte.getEntry(entite).getLoadedValue(propriete)

// entities in the session's persistence context (Hibernate's internal API)
private fun Session.afficherEntitesSuivies() {
    for ((entite, entree) in contexte.reentrantSafeEntityEntries()) {
        val persister = entree.persister
        println("${persister.entityName} #${entree.id} ${entree.status}")
         // current property values, compared to the values read from the database
        val actuelles = persister.getValues(entite)
        val origines = entree.loadedState
        persister.propertyNames.forEachIndexed { i, nom ->
            val modification = if (actuelles[i] == origines[i]) ""
                else " (modifiée, valeur d'origine : ${origines[i]})"
            println("    $nom : ${actuelles[i]}$modification")
        }
    }
    println("session modifiée : $isDirty")
}
