    Comments:

    • Line 17: [session.find(Article::class.java, 1)] searches for the primary key record 1. It returns [null] if the key does not exist; the operator [?:] then throws an exception ([error], Chapter 3), and [velo] is of type [Article], which is non-nullable. The generated SQL (lines 3–6 of the results) is a parameterized [SELECT], whose parameter is set to 1: the compact log now displays the parameter values;
    • line 20: the second call to [find(Article::class.java, 1)] does not send any SQL commands and returns the same object (line 9). The [===] operator compares references (the Java [] operator), whereas [] would call [equals] (Chapter 3). The session stores the entities it has read or saved in its persistence context—also known as the first-level cache: before querying the database, [find] checks to see if the requested entity is already there. A session never contains two objects for the same row in the database;
    • Lines 25–29: adding an item. Before [persist], the object is [TRANSIENT] (“transient”): the session does not recognize it, and its identifier is [null] (line 12). [persist] brings it into the session, which immediately executes the command [INSERT] (lines 13–18) to obtain the generated key, and places it in the field [id] (Hibernate writes to the field directly: the property’s protected modifier does not prevent this). The item is then [MANAGED] (“managed” or “persistent”), and its identifier is 7 (line 19). The transaction is opened at the beginning of the block [inTransaction] and committed at its end (lines 11 and 20 of the results). The block parameter ([Transaction]) is not used: it is not named;
    • line 35: to modify a row in the database, simply modify the object. No [update] method is required: the session has retained a copy of the read or saved values (the original state) and compares the current values to those. This is known as “dirty checking.” The [*=] operator is translated here by Kotlin into [x.prix = x.prix * BigDecimal("1.1")]: a new [BigDecimal] object (which is immutable) is assigned to the property;
    • Lines 36–37: The property [isDirty] (the Java method [isDirty()]) indicates whether the session contains changes that have not yet been committed to the database: this is the case (line 23). The function [valeurOrigine] (lines 84–85) reads the original price value, 100, from the persistence context, whereas the current value is 110.0;
    • line 38: the end of the block. The subsequent [commit] synchronizes the session with the database (“flush”): the [UPDATE] command is executed (lines 25–32), and then the transaction is committed. After that, the session has no pending changes (line 34);
    • Note that the [UPDATE] command writes all columns in the table, not just the one that has changed. This is Hibernate’s default behavior: a single SQL command, prepared once and for all, is used for all article modifications. In contrast, the [@DynamicUpdate] annotation placed on the entity instructs it to generate a query limited to the modified columns each time;
    • Lines 45–48: deletion. [remove] changes the article’s status to [DELETED] (line 37); [commit] sends the command [DELETE] (lines 38–40). The object is then no longer recognized by the session: it becomes [DETACHED] (“detached,” line 42);
    • lines 52–55: the arc is read (lines 44–47), then detached from the session by [detach]: the session forgets it (line 48). Any change to its price is then ignored. A detached object is a common occurrence in an application: it is an object read by a session that is now closed—for example, during a previous HTTP query—and subsequently modified by the user;
    • line 57: [session.merge(arc)] merges the detached object with the session. The session reads the item from the database (lines 50–53), copies the state of the detached object into the entity it manages, and returns the latter: this is not the same object (line 54). The object passed to [merge] remains detached; the returned object is the one that must be used next. [commit] records the new price (lines 55–62);
    • line 64: the bike’s inventory is updated, without a transaction;
    • lines 71–72: the session’s persistence context, obtained via an extension property: in the following functions, [contexte] is treated as a session property. [unwrap] provides access to the session’s internal interface [SessionImplementor];
    • lines 75–80: the status of an item, calculated by a [when] without arguments. First, [isEntryFor] is used to check whether the session is associated with the item: the [getEntry] method, which returns [null] for an unknown object (which is what the Java code tests for), is nevertheless annotated as [@NonNull] in Hibernate. Kotlin takes these nullability annotations from the Java libraries into account: it considers that [getEntry] returns a non-nullable [EntityEntry] and flags a check for [?.] on its result (“[unnecessary safe call on a non-null receiver of type 'EntityEntry'.]”) as unnecessary ( a warning, and thus an error with our compilation options). This is a rare but instructive case: the types in a Java library are always exactly what their annotations specify;
    • Lines 88–101: display of the persistence context. For each tracked entity ([EntityEntry]), its name, identifier, and state are displayed, followed by the current value of each property and its original value if it differs. The [EntityPersister] object is the one in Hibernate that knows the mapping between an entity and its table: it provides the names of the properties and their values. The [for ((entite, entree) in ...)] loop unpacks each element of the array, a [Map.Entry] (Chapter 5); [forEachIndexed] iterates over the property names along with their indices. The [==] operator between two values—which can be [null]—replaces Java’s [Objects.equals]. In an extension function, [isDirty] refers to the receiver’s property, the session;
    • Lines 65–75 of the results: The session tracks the bike, whose stock has changed from 10 to 9, and the arc. The change to the bike is not saved: the session is closed without synchronization. There is no [commit], and a session does not synchronize automatically upon closure.

    11.5.2. The States of an Entity

    An entity is, with respect to a session, in one of the following states (Jakarta Persistence refers to them as “new,” “managed,” “detached,” and “removed”):

    State
    Meaning
    transient ([TRANSIENT])
    The object was created by a constructor call and has never been registered: it has no identifier, and no session is aware of it
    Managed ([MANAGED])
    The object has been read or saved by the session, which is tracking it: changes to it will be reflected in the database during the next synchronization
    Deleted ([DELETED])
    The object has been marked for deletion ([remove]): the next synchronization will send the command [DELETE]
    detached ([DETACHED])
    The object corresponds to a row in the database, but the session that read it is closed or has forgotten it ([detach], [clear]): its changes are ignored unless it is merged with a session ([merge])

    Synchronizing (“flushing”) the session sends the SQL commands to SGBD, which propagate the changes to the managed entities. This occurs:

    • during the [commit] phase of the transaction;
    • before executing a query whose result might depend on changes that have not yet been committed ([FlushMode.AUTO] mode, the default mode): the query thus sees the session data;
    • during an explicit call to [session.flush()]. The commands are then executed, but they will not be permanently saved until the transaction’s [commit].

    Here’s an overview of the workflow with Hibernate: we open a session and a transaction, read entities, modify them as ordinary objects, add them ([persist]), and delete them ([remove]), then commit the transaction, which sends all necessary commands to the database in a single batch. The session acts as a “unit of work.” It is a lightweight object designed for a short lifespan: a unit of work, such as a HTTP request in a web application. You do not use the same session throughout the entire lifetime of an application—it would accumulate the tracked entities in its persistence context.

    In Kotlin, this cycle is naturally implemented using Hibernate’s higher-order functions: [sessionFactory.inTransaction { session -> ... }] for a complete unit of work (session and transaction), [sessionFactory.fromTransaction { session -> ... }] when it returns a result, and [session.inTransaction { ... }] for a transaction within an already open session. In short, these are the equivalents of the [use] function for transactions.

    11.6. The queries HQL

    11.6.1. HQL and JPQL

    To retrieve entities other than by their primary key, queries are written in a language similar to SQL, but one that refers to entities and attributes rather than tables and columns: HQL (Hibernate Query Language). Jakarta Persistence defines a similar language, JPQL (Jakarta Persistence Query Language), of which HQL is a superset: a JPQL query is a valid HQL query. Hibernate translates the query into SQL, in the SGBD dialect, and it is SGBD that executes it.

    Some differences from SQL:

    • We use the entity name ([Article]), not the table name ([articles]), and the attribute names ([stockActuel]), not the column names. Entity and attribute names are case-sensitive, just like in Kotlin. With our Kotlin entities, an attribute’s name is the same as the property’s name (Hibernate accesses the field that stores it, and that field is named after the property);
    • the clause [select] is optional in HQL: [from Article] returns entities [Article]. JPQL requires writing [select a from Article a];
    • relationships between entities are traversed using a dot ([p.categorie.nom]), with Hibernate writing the joins itself, as we will see.

    A query is created by the session's [createSelectionQuery] method, which receives the text HQL and the result type ([Article::class.java], the Java class of the entity), and returns a [SelectionQuery<T>] object. You can then assign values to its parameters and execute it with [getResultList] (a list), [getSingleResult] (a single result; an exception if there are zero or more), [getSingleResultOrNull] ([null] if there are none), or [getResultStream] (a stream). As is always the case with Java classes, Kotlin allows you to write these parameterless [getXxx] methods as properties: [query.resultList], [query.singleResult], [query.singleResultOrNull]. The [createQuery] method from Jakarta Persistence also exists; it is used for both read queries and updates.

    package hql

import articles.Article
import articles.BaseArticles
import org.hibernate.query.SemanticException
import java.math.BigDecimal

// the queries HQL / JPQL on the table [articles]

// a projection: the name of an item and its stock value (a data class, not an entity)
data class ValeurStock(val nom: String, val valeur: BigDecimal)

// a business rule written in Kotlin (an extension function):
// an item is out of stock if its inventory is below the minimum inventory level
fun Article.enRupture() = stockActuel < stockMinimum

fun main() {
    BaseArticles.creerSessionFactory().use { sessionFactory ->
         // the table [articles] is recreated with its six items
        BaseArticles.initialiser(sessionFactory)
        sessionFactory.openSession().use { session ->
             // 1 - filtering and sorting
            println("--- les articles à réapprovisionner, par ordre alphabétique")
            val hql = "from Article where stockActuel < stockMinimum order by nom"
            val aCommander = session.createSelectionQuery(hql, Article::class.java).resultList
            aCommander.forEach(::println)

             // 2 - projection: only the relevant columns are retrieved
            println("--- valeur du stock de chaque article")
            val valeurs = session
                .createSelectionQuery(
                    """
                    select nom, prix * stockActuel from Article
                    order by prix * stockActuel desc""", ValeurStock::class.java
                )
                .resultList
            for ((nom, valeur) in valeurs) {
                println("%s : %.2f euros".format(nom, valeur))
            }

             // 3 - a single result; the value [prixMin] is passed via a named parameter
            println("--- le premier article de plus de 200 euros")
            val prixMin = BigDecimal(200)
            val article: Article? = session
                .createSelectionQuery(
                    """
                    select a from Article a
                    where a.prix > :prixMin order by a.prix""", Article::class.java
                )
                .setParameter("prixMin", prixMin)
                .setMaxResults(1)
                .singleResultOrNull
            println(article ?: "aucun")

             // 4 - aggregates: the calculation is performed by SGBD
            println("--- agrégats")
            val nbArticles = session
                .createSelectionQuery("select count(*) from Article", Long::class.java)
                .singleResult
            val valeurStock = session
                .createSelectionQuery("select sum(prix * stockActuel) from Article", BigDecimal::class.java)
                .singleResult
            println("%d articles, valeur du stock : %.2f euros".format(nbArticles, valeurStock))

             // 5 - `like` and `in`; a Kotlin list as the value of a parameter
            println("--- like et in")
            val noms = listOf("arc", "pompe", "raquette")
            val resultats = session
                .createSelectionQuery(
                    """
                    select nom from Article
                    where nom like 'b%' or nom in :noms""", String::class.java
                )
                .setParameter("noms", noms)
                .resultList
            println(resultats.joinToString(", "))

             // 6 - pagination: the third page of two articles, sorted by price in ascending order
            println("--- pagination")
            val taillePage = 2
            val numeroPage = 3
            val page = session.createSelectionQuery("from Article order by prix", Article::class.java)
                .setFirstResult((numeroPage - 1) * taillePage)
                .setMaxResults(taillePage)
                .resultList
            val texte = page.joinToString(", ") { "%s (%.2f euros)".format(it.nom, it.prix) }
            println("page $numeroPage : $texte")

             // 7 - An invalid query is rejected as soon as it is created, before execution
            println("--- requête incorrecte")
            try {
                session.createSelectionQuery("from Article where stock < stockMinimum", Article::class.java)
            } catch (e: SemanticException) {
                println("${e.javaClass.simpleName} : ${e.message}")
            }

             // 8 - A rule written in Kotlin cannot be translated into SQL: in-memory filtering
            println("--- filtrage en mémoire")
            session.createSelectionQuery("from Article", Article::class.java).resultStream.use { flux ->
                flux.filter { it.enRupture() }.forEach(::println)
            }
        }
    }
}

    Comments:

    • Lines 24–26: The clause [where] compares two attributes of the entity; the clause [order by] sorts by name: they become the clauses [WHERE] and [ORDER BY] in the order SQL. The query is executed by [resultList] (the [getResultList] method), which returns a [List<Article>]; [forEach(::println)] displays each item using its method [toString];
    • Lines 30–38: a projection. The query does not return entities, but rather two values per item: the name and the stock value. The generated SQL retrieves only the necessary columns and performs the calculation itself. The result type is the [ValeurStock] data class from line 11: Hibernate creates one object per row, passing the values from the [select] clause to its constructor in order (the Java course used a record). These objects are not entities: the session does not track them. A data class is perfectly suited for this role, and we take advantage of its destructuring: [for ((nom, valeur) in valeurs)] (line 37);
    • lines 32–34: the query is written in a raw string (["""..."""], Chapter 5), which is more readable than a long string on a single line. Unlike Java text blocks, a raw string preserves its line indentation and the initial line break; this is irrelevant here, since spaces and line breaks do not matter in HQL: there is no need to call [trimIndent];
    • lines 44–53: a query written as in JPQL, with an alias ([a]). [:prixMin] is a named parameter, whose value is given by [setParameter]. It becomes a parameter of the order SQL (the [?] from the clause [WHERE], whose value is displayed by the log): so there is no need to worry about SQL injections, since the value is passed separately from the order text. This is the rule that Chapter 10 applied to prepared statements. [setMaxResults(1)] limits the result to a single row: the [LIMIT] clause of MySQL. [singleResultOrNull] returns a [Article?]: the nullable type clearly states that there may be no result, and the Elvis operator [?:] displays [aucun] in this case;
    • It’s important to highlight a pitfall specific to Kotlin. Its string templates make it very tempting to write ["... where a.prix > $prixMin"]. The program would work, but the value would then be copied into the query text: it is precisely this concatenation that opens the door to injections (Chapter 10), and Hibernate would have to parse a new query for each value. We never use the character [$] to set a value in a query HQL: values are passed via named parameters. A literal value written in the query text (such as ['b%'] on line 72) is also copied into the text of the SQL command, as shown in the log: this is acceptable for a program constant, but never for a value coming from an external source;
    • Lines 57–63: The aggregates [count] and [sum] are calculated by SGBD: only the result is transferred, not the rows. [Long::class.java] refers to the class of the primitive type [long] in Java (the Kotlin type [Long] is compiled to [long]), whereas the Java course used [Long.class], the wrapper class [java.lang.Long]; Hibernate accepts both (the wrapper class would be written as [Long::class.javaObjectType]). HQL also recognizes [avg], [min], [max], the clauses [group by] and [having];
    • lines 67–76: the [like] operator of SQL, and the [in] operator, whose operand is a parameter that accepts a Kotlin list (a Kotlin [List] is a Hibernate [java.util.List]): Hibernate expands it into as many SQL parameters as there are elements in the list. HQL supports numerous functions on strings ([upper], [length], [substring]...), dates, and numbers, which it translates into the SGBD dialect;
    • lines 82–85: pagination, to display a long list page by page. [setFirstResult] skips the entries from the previous pages, while [setMaxResults] keeps those from the requested page: the [LIMIT ?, ?] clause of MySQL, whose two parameters are 4 and 2. Pagination only makes sense on a sorted list ([order by]). Lines 86–87 construct the page display using [joinToString] and its transformation function (Chapter 5);
    • lines 91–94: a query that uses a [stock] attribute that does not exist. The error is detected as soon as the query is created, before any execution, because Hibernate parses the text HQL and compares it to the model: it throws a [SemanticException] (Hibernate messages are in English). A syntax error would result in a [SyntaxException]. Note that the value returned by [createSelectionQuery] is ignored: in Kotlin, there is no requirement to use the result of a function;
    • lines 15 and 99–100: a query cannot use a Kotlin function, such as the extension function [enRupture]: Hibernate does not know its code, and even if it did, it would not necessarily know how to write it as SQL. You can read all entities and filter them in memory: [resultStream] (the [getResultStream] method) returns a Java [Stream<Article>], which holds a JDBC resource open and must be closed after use: the [use] function handles this, since a [Stream] is a [AutoCloseable]. The result is correct, but the entire table was transferred (the last SQL order has no [WHERE] clause): with a large table, this should be avoided. It’s better to write the condition in the query, as shown on line 24. The extension function also demonstrates a very “Kotlin”-like way of writing a business rule on an entity without modifying its class (Chapter 4).

    11.6.3. Named Queries and Compile-Time Validation

    A query written in a string is only parsed at runtime. There are two ways to detect errors earlier:

    • Named queries: The [@NamedQuery(name = "Article.enRupture", query = "from Article where stockActuel < stockMinimum")] annotation, applied to the entity, declares a query that Hibernate parses at startup, when creating the [SessionFactory]. It is then executed by its name: [session.createNamedSelectionQuery("Article.enRupture", Article::class.java)]. It is written in Kotlin exactly the same way as in Java; the annotation is repeatable: it is applied as many times as there are queries to declare;
    • the Hibernate annotation processor (“Hibernate Processor,” library [org.hibernate.orm:hibernate-processor]). In Java, it is executed by [javac] during compilation: it checks the queries in the annotations and generates, for each entity, a “metamodel” class ([Article_] for [Article]), which we’ll see again with the API Criteria. This mechanism does not apply solely to Kotlin: we’ll return to this below when discussing the static metamodel.

    11.7. The API Criteria

    11.7.1. Queries Built with Code

    A HQL query is a string that can be constructed through concatenation (or, in Kotlin, using templates): this approach is unreliable and hard to read as soon as the query depends on many optional criteria (a search form, for example). Jakarta Persistence offers another way to write queries: API Criteria, where the query is a tree of objects built through method calls. Hibernate translates this tree into SQL, just like a HQL query (it also translates HQL into such a tree). The subproject [criteria] (its [build.gradle.kts] is that of the subproject [hql], except for the program name) includes several queries from the previous program:

    package criteria

import articles.Article
import articles.BaseArticles
import jakarta.persistence.criteria.Path
import jakarta.persistence.criteria.Predicate
import org.hibernate.Session
import java.math.BigDecimal
import kotlin.reflect.KProperty1

// queries built with the API Criteria

// a projection: the name of an item and its stock value
data class ValeurStock(val nom: String, val valeur: BigDecimal)

// an attribute denoted by a property reference (Article::price), not by a string ("price"):
// the name is validated by the compiler, and the type of the rendered path is that of the property
fun <X, T> Path<X>.get(propriete: KProperty1<X, T>): Path<T> = get(propriete.name)

fun main() {
    BaseArticles.creerSessionFactory().use { sessionFactory ->
         // the table [articles] is recreated with its six items
        BaseArticles.initialiser(sessionFactory)
        sessionFactory.openSession().use { session ->
             // the factory for query elements
            val cb = session.criteriaBuilder

             // 1 - filtering and sorting; attributes are designated by strings
            println("--- les articles à réapprovisionner, par ordre alphabétique")
            val requete = cb.createQuery(Article::class.java)
            val a = requete.from(Article::class.java)
            requete.select(a)
                .where(cb.lt(a.get<Int>("stockActuel"), a.get<Int>("stockMinimum")))
                .orderBy(cb.asc(a.get<String>("nom")))
            session.createSelectionQuery(requete).resultList.forEach(::println)

             // 2 - projection onto a data class; attributes are designated by references
            println("--- valeur du stock de chaque article")
            val projection = cb.createQuery(ValeurStock::class.java)
            val p = projection.from(Article::class.java)
            val valeur = cb.prod(p.get(Article::prix), p.get(Article::stockActuel))
                .`as`(BigDecimal::class.java)
            projection.select(cb.construct(ValeurStock::class.java, p.get(Article::nom), valeur))
                .orderBy(cb.desc(valeur))
            for ((nom, v) in session.createSelectionQuery(projection).resultList) {
                println("%s : %.2f euros".format(nom, v))
            }

             // 3 - A query constructed according to the provided criteria
            println("--- recherche : prix maximal 150 euros")
            rechercher(session, prixMax = BigDecimal(150)).forEach(::println)
            println("--- recherche : prix maximal 150 euros et nom commençant par [b]")
            rechercher(session, prixMax = BigDecimal(150), debutNom = "b").forEach(::println)

             // 4 - aggregates
            println("--- agrégats")
            val compte = cb.createQuery(Long::class.java)
            compte.select(cb.count(compte.from(Article::class.java)))
            val nbArticles = session.createSelectionQuery(compte).singleResult
            val somme = cb.createQuery(BigDecimal::class.java)
            val s = somme.from(Article::class.java)
            val valeurArticle = cb.prod(s.get(Article::prix), s.get(Article::stockActuel))
                .`as`(BigDecimal::class.java)
            somme.select(cb.sum(valeurArticle))
            val valeurStock = session.createSelectionQuery(somme).singleResult
            println("%d articles, valeur du stock : %.2f euros".format(nbArticles, valeurStock))
        }
    }
}

// items whose price does not exceed [prixMax] and whose name begins with [debutNom],
// each criterion is used only if it is not null
fun rechercher(session: Session, prixMax: BigDecimal? = null, debutNom: String? = null): List<Article> {
    val cb = session.criteriaBuilder
    val requete = cb.createQuery(Article::class.java)
    val a = requete.from(Article::class.java)
     // the conditions, added one by one
    val conditions = buildList<Predicate> {
        prixMax?.let { add(cb.le(a.get(Article::prix), it)) }
        debutNom?.let { add(cb.like(a.get(Article::nom), "$it%")) }
    }
    requete.select(a).where(conditions).orderBy(cb.asc(a.get(Article::prix)))
    return session.createSelectionQuery(requete).resultList
}

    Comments:

    • line 26: the session returns a [HibernateCriteriaBuilder] ([criteriaBuilder], the [getCriteriaBuilder] method), the Hibernate-enhanced version of Jakarta Persistence’s [CriteriaBuilder]: This is the factory for all elements of a query (conditions, expressions, sorts);
    • lines 30–34: the query from the first example, HQL. [createQuery(Article::class.java)] creates a query that returns articles; [from(Article::class.java)] declares the queried entity and returns its root ([Root<Article>]), which is the equivalent of the alias [a] for [from Article a]; [a.get<Int>("stockActuel")] designates an attribute. The condition is constructed by [cb.lt(x, y)] (“less than,” [x < y]), and the sort by [cb.asc(...)]. The explicit type argument [<Int>] (in Java: [a.<Integer>get(...)]) specifies the attribute’s type, which cannot be determined from the string ["stockActuel"]. The compiler cannot verify that it is correct: it takes our word for it;
    • line 35: the query is executed by the session, as a HQL query. The generated SQL is the same as that of the HQL query;
    • line 18: an extension function of the Jakarta Persistence interface [Path], which refers to an attribute using a property reference ([Article::prix], of type [KProperty1<Article, BigDecimal>], Chapter 7) rather than a string. It simply passes the property name ([propriete.name], here ["prix"]) to the original [get] method, but it provides two guarantees: the compiler verifies that the property exists, and the type of the rendered path ([Path<BigDecimal>]) is inferred from that of the property, without an explicit type argument. This relies on the fact that the attribute name JPA is the same as the Kotlin property name, which is the case for our entities;
    • Lines 39–46: a projection to the data class [ValeurStock], using the extension function: [p.get(Article::prix)]. [cb.prod(x, y)] is the product of two expressions; [as(BigDecimal::class.java)] specifies the result type ([as] is a Kotlin keyword: to call the Java method with this name, it is enclosed in grave accents); [cb.construct(ValeurStock::class.java, ...)] indicates that each line of the result must be passed to the data class’s constructor;
    • Lines 73–83: This is where the API Criteria function is most useful. The [rechercher] function constructs a query based on the criteria provided. Its criteria are nullable parameters with a default value ([prixMax: BigDecimal? = null]), which allows for the named-argument calls in lines 51 and 53 (in Java, [null] had to be passed explicitly). The list of conditions is constructed by [buildList]: each condition is added to it only if the corresponding criterion is not [null] ([prixMax?.let { ... \}]), and the clause [where] receives the entire list ([where(conditions)], an overhead introduced with Jakarta Persistence 3.2), with the conditions combined by [and]. The first call produces a query with one condition; the second produces a query with two conditions. Note that with the API Criteria, Hibernate passes the values ([150], [b%]) as parameters in the order SQL: the template ["$it%"] on line 80 constructs the valeur for the parameter (the pattern for [like]), not the query text;
    • Lines 57–64: the aggregates [count] and [sum].

    11.7.2. The Static Metamodel

    The weakness of the queries in the first example is that attributes are designated by strings ([a.get<Int>("stockActuel")]): a typo will not be detected until runtime, and the compiler ignores the attribute’s type. To address this, Jakarta Persistence provides a static metamodel: for each entity [Article], there is a class [Article_] that contains one field per attribute, describing its name and type. In Java, you then write ***[cb.lt(a.get(Article\_.stockActuel), a.get(Article\_.stockMinimum))]***, which the compiler fully validates. These classes are not written by hand: they are generated during compilation by Hibernate’s annotation processor. This is the recommended approach in a Java project that uses the API Criteria.

    In Kotlin, it’s not quite that simple. The Hibernate annotation processor is a Java annotation processor: it is executed by [javac] on Java source code, but our entities are compiled by the Kotlin compiler. The Kotlin tool for this type of code generation is KSP (Kotlin Symbol Processing), but Hibernate does not provide a KSP processor. That leaves kapt (“Kotlin annotation processing tool”), which runs Java processors on “stubs ” generated from Kotlin code; however, kapt is in maintenance mode at JetBrains (which recommends KSP), it slows down compilation, and the kapt + Hibernate Processor combination is not a configuration documented by Hibernate. Therefore, we do not use it. Kotlin’s property references provide much of the benefit without any tools: with the program’s extension function, a typo is detected at compile time. Here’s what the compiler says for [a.get(Article::stock)], compiled into a test file:

    1
2
3
    Faute.kt:9:50: error: unresolved reference 'stock'.
fun condition(a: Path<Article>) = a.get(Article::stock)
                                                 ^^^^^

    (The compiler also displays, beforehand, the list of candidate [get] methods, none of which are suitable.) However, the check is not comprehensive: a Kotlin property that is not a persistent attribute (a computed property, for example) would be accepted by the compiler but rejected by Hibernate at runtime.

    For a fixed query, HQL is more readable than the API Criteria; for a query that is constructed based on the circumstances, the API Criteria is safer. The two can be combined: Hibernate allows you to create a Criteria query from a HQL ([cb.createQuery(hql, Article::class.java)]) string and then supplement it with code.

    11.8. Relationships

    11.8.1. The Store Model

    The tables in a database are linked to one another. Hibernate represents these links as associations: properties that reference another entity or a collection of entities. The [relations] subproject uses a [hbboutique] database that describes a small store with six entities. Since it defines entities, its [build.gradle.kts] applies the [jpa] and [allopen] plugins, just like the one in the [articles] library; it depends directly on the [outils] library (the SQL log), Hibernate, and the MySQL driver:

plugins {
    kotlin("jvm")
     // the parameterless constructor for entities (the “no-arg” plugin set to JPA)
    kotlin("plugin.jpa")
     // Entities and properties set to open (non-final): Hibernate can derive proxies from them
    kotlin("plugin.allopen")
    application
}

repositories {
    mavenCentral()
}

dependencies {
     // the compact SQL log (and Logback)
    implementation(project(":outils"))
     // Hibernate and the JDBC driver from MySQL
    implementation("org.hibernate.orm:hibernate-core:7.4.5.Final")
    runtimeOnly("com.mysql:mysql-connector-j:9.7.0")
}

// Classes annotated in this way are loaded by the [allopen] plugin
allOpen {
    annotation("jakarta.persistence.Entity")
    annotation("jakarta.persistence.MappedSuperclass")
    annotation("jakarta.persistence.Embeddable")
}

kotlin {
    jvmToolchain(25)
    compilerOptions {
        allWarningsAsErrors = true
        javaParameters = true
    }
}

application {
     // The program executed by [gradlew -q :relations:run]
    mainClass = "relations.MainKt"
}

// otherwise accented characters are garbled in the console of IntelliJ IDEA or the terminal
tasks.withType<JavaExec>().configureEach {
    jvmArgs("-Dstdout.encoding=UTF-8", "-Dstderr.encoding=UTF-8")
}

    package relations

import jakarta.persistence.CascadeType
import jakarta.persistence.Column
import jakarta.persistence.Entity
import jakarta.persistence.GeneratedValue
import jakarta.persistence.GenerationType
import jakarta.persistence.Id
import jakarta.persistence.OneToMany
import jakarta.persistence.Table

// A category groups together several products (one-to-many relationship)
@Entity
@Table(name = "categories")
class Categorie(
    @Column(nullable = false, length = 30)
    var nom: String,
) {
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    var id: Int? = null
        protected set

     // Products in the category: the inverse side of the relationship, described by Produit.categorie
    @OneToMany(mappedBy = "categorie", cascade = [CascadeType.PERSIST])
    val produits: MutableList<Produit> = mutableListOf()

     // Adding a product: both sides of the relationship are updated
    fun ajouter(produit: Produit) {
        produits += produit
        produit.categorie = this
    }
}

import jakarta.persistence.CascadeType
import jakarta.persistence.Column
import jakarta.persistence.Entity
import jakarta.persistence.FetchType
import jakarta.persistence.ForeignKey
import jakarta.persistence.GeneratedValue
import jakarta.persistence.GenerationType
import jakarta.persistence.Id
import jakarta.persistence.JoinColumn
import jakarta.persistence.JoinTable
import jakarta.persistence.ManyToMany
import jakarta.persistence.ManyToOne
import jakarta.persistence.Table
import java.math.BigDecimal

// A product belongs to a category and has multiple tags
@Entity
@Table(name = "produits")
class Produit(
    @Column(nullable = false, length = 30)
    var nom: String,
    @Column(nullable = false, precision = 10, scale = 2)
    var prix: BigDecimal,
    vararg etiquettes: Etiquette,
) {
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    var id: Int? = null
        protected set

     // many-to-one relationship: the foreign key [categorie_id] from the table [produits]
     // [lateinit]: the category is populated after creation by Categorie.ajouter
    @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY, optional = false)
    @JoinColumn(name = "categorie_id", foreignKey = ForeignKey(name = "fk_produits_categorie"))
    lateinit var categorie: Categorie
        internal set

     // many-to-many relationship, stored in an association table
    @ManyToMany(cascade = [CascadeType.PERSIST])
    @JoinTable(
        name = "produits_etiquettes",
        joinColumns = [JoinColumn(name = "produit_id")],
        inverseJoinColumns = [JoinColumn(name = "etiquette_id")],
        foreignKey = ForeignKey(name = "fk_produits_etiquettes_produit"),
        inverseForeignKey = ForeignKey(name = "fk_produits_etiquettes_etiquette"),
    )
    val etiquettes: MutableSet<Etiquette> = mutableSetOf()

    init {
         // only the owner side of the relationship is populated: this is the one that Hibernate saves
        this.etiquettes += etiquettes
    }
}

import jakarta.persistence.Entity
import jakarta.persistence.FetchType
import jakarta.persistence.GeneratedValue
import jakarta.persistence.GenerationType
import jakarta.persistence.Id
import jakarta.persistence.JoinColumn
import jakarta.persistence.ManyToOne
import jakarta.persistence.Table

// an order line: a quantity of a product
@Entity
@Table(name = "lignes_commande")
class LigneCommande(
    @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY, optional = false)
    @JoinColumn(name = "produit_id")
    var produit: Produit,
    var quantite: Int,
) {
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    var id: Int? = null
        protected set

    @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY, optional = false)
    @JoinColumn(name = "commande_id")
    lateinit var commande: Commande
        internal set
}

    It contains three types of associations:

    • a many-to-one relationship ([@ManyToOne]): a product belongs to a category (the property [categorie] of [Produit]). In the database, this is represented by a foreign key, the column [categorie_id] in the table [produits], where [@JoinColumn] specifies the name and the constraint name ([fk_produits_categorie]). [optional = false] makes the relationship mandatory: the column will be [NOT NULL]. Note the syntax for nested annotations in Kotlin: an annotation passed as an argument to another is written without [@] ([foreignKey = ForeignKey(name = ...)]), and an array of annotations is written in square brackets ([joinColumns = [JoinColumn(name = "produit_id")]]), such as the array [cascade = [CascadeType.PERSIST]];
    • the inverse, one-to-many relationship ([@OneToMany]): a category contains multiple products (the property [produits] of [Categorie]). It does not create anything in the database: [mappedBy = "categorie"] indicates that it is described by the property [categorie] of the entity [Produit]. [Produit.categorie] is said to be the owner side of the relationship, and [Categorie.produits] its inverse side: Hibernate stores the value of the owner side. However, both sides must be kept consistent in memory: this is the role of the function [ajouter] of [Categorie], which adds the product to the list ([produits += produit], the [+=] operator for a mutable collection, Chapter 5) and sets its category;
    • a many-to-many relationship ([@ManyToMany]): a product has multiple labels, and a label is associated with multiple products. It is stored in an association table, [produits_etiquettes], for which [@JoinTable] specifies the name, the names of the two columns, and the names of the two foreign keys (the property [etiquettes] of [Produit]). The reverse side is [Etiquette.produits] ([mappedBy = "etiquettes"]). For a many-to-many relationship, a set ([MutableSet]) is preferred over a list ([MutableList]): with a list, Hibernate deletes and re-inserts all rows in the association table every time the collection is modified;
    • [fetch = FetchType.LAZY] requests lazy loading of a product’s category: it will only be read when it is used. This is the default behavior for collections ([@OneToMany], [@ManyToMany]), but not for relationships to a single entity ([@ManyToOne]), which the standard loads immediately by default ([EAGER]): [fetch = FetchType.LAZY] is systematically added to them, as recommended by the Hibernate documentation;
    • [cascade = [CascadeType.PERSIST]] propagates the operation [persist]: persisting a category persists its products, and persisting a product persists its tags. The other values ([MERGE], [REMOVE], [ALL]...) propagate the other operations.

    The transition to Kotlin warrants several comments:

    • Collections are declared using Kotlin's mutable interfaces, [MutableList] and [MutableSet], which are initialized by [mutableListOf()] and [mutableSetOf()]. This choice is mandatory: Hibernate replaces the collection of an entity it reads with its own collection (a [PersistentBag] or a [PersistentSet]), which is a mutable [java.util.List] or [java.util.Set], and which can be loaded on demand. A read-only [List] from Kotlin would be acceptable to the compiler, but it would not accurately represent an object that Hibernate and the [ajouter] function modify. Properties are [val]: we modify the contents of the collection, never the reference;
    • a relationship to a single entity, which is required, is declared as [lateinit var categorie: Categorie] (in [Produit]; the same applies to [Commande.client] and [LigneCommande.commande]). The type is not nullable, because a registered product always has a category; however, at the time of its creation, it does not yet have one: [Categorie.ajouter] will populate it. [lateinit] expresses exactly that: the property will be initialized later, and reading it before then would throw a [UninitializedPropertyAccessException], which is more descriptive than a [NullPointerException]. The Java course had relied on [null] up until then. We could also have written [var categorie: Categorie? = null], at the cost of having to use [?.] or [!!] each time;
    • the modifier [internal set] placed under these properties reserves the modification of a product’s category (of an order’s customer, of an order’s line item) for the module—that is, for the Gradle subproject [relations]: only the function [ajouter] uses it. In Java, the method [setCategorie] was visible only within the package; Kotlin does not have “package” visibility, and [internal] is the closest equivalent;
    • A product’s labels are passed to its constructor via a parameter named [vararg], which is not a property (there is no [val] or [var]): it is used only in the block [init], which adds them to the set. In this block, [etiquettes] refers to the parameter and [this.etiquettes] to the property; the block [init] is placed after the property declaration, because initializations are executed in the order they appear in the text. The operator [+=] adds all elements of an array to a mutable collection;
    • the parameterless constructor added by the [jpa] plugin (the one Hibernate uses to create the entities it reads) does not execute property initializations: the [etiquettes] collection for a product read by Hibernate is therefore not created by [mutableSetOf()]. This is not a problem, because Hibernate itself populates all associations for the entities it reads using its lazy-loaded collections;
    • entities remain ordinary classes, not data classes. Relationships provide yet another reason for this: the functions [toString], [equals], and [hashCode] generated for a data class all use the properties of its primary constructor; if they included associations, they would iterate over the lazy collections (triggering queries or a [LazyInitializationException] outside the session), and two entities that reference each other would call each other indefinitely ([StackOverflowError]);
    • Finally, the [allopen] plugin is essential here: for a lazy relationship to a single entity, Hibernate places a proxy—an object of a subclass of the entity generated at runtime—in the property, which requires that the class and its accessors be non-final. We’ll see this proxy in action in the program.

    package relations

import org.hibernate.SessionFactory
import org.hibernate.cfg.AvailableSettings
import org.hibernate.jpa.HibernatePersistenceConfiguration
import outils.JournalSql
import java.math.BigDecimal
import java.time.LocalDate

// the database [hbboutique]: Hibernate configuration and first dataset
object Boutique {

     // a SessionFactory for the database [hbboutique] and its six entities
    fun creerSessionFactory(): SessionFactory =
        HibernatePersistenceConfiguration("boutique")
            .managedClasses(
                Categorie::class.java, Produit::class.java, Etiquette::class.java,
                Client::class.java, Commande::class.java, LigneCommande::class.java,
            )
            .jdbcUrl("jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/hbboutique?createDatabaseIfNotExist=true")
            .jdbcCredentials("root", "")
            .property(AvailableSettings.FORMAT_SQL, true)
            .createEntityManagerFactory()

     // (re)creation of tables and an initial dataset, without a log SQL
    fun initialiser(sessionFactory: SessionFactory) = JournalSql.sansJournal {
        sessionFactory.schemaManager.drop(false)
        sessionFactory.schemaManager.create(false)
        sessionFactory.inTransaction { session ->
             // two labels
            val promo = Etiquette("promo")
            val nouveaute = Etiquette("nouveauté")
             // three categories and their products: an object graph
            val cycles = Categorie("cycles")
            cycles.ajouter(Produit("vélo", BigDecimal(500), promo))
            val pompe = Produit("pompe", BigDecimal(10))
            cycles.ajouter(pompe)
            val tirALArc = Categorie("tir à l'arc")
            val arc = Produit("arc", BigDecimal(600), nouveaute)
            tirALArc.ajouter(arc)
            tirALArc.ajouter(Produit("flèches - lot de 6", BigDecimal(100), promo, nouveaute))
            val plongee = Categorie("plongée")
             // Persistence propagates to products and labels (cascade)
            session.persist(cycles)
            session.persist(tirALArc)
            session.persist(plongee)
             // a customer and their two-line order
            val commande = Commande(LocalDate.of(2026, 9, 28))
            commande.ajouter(LigneCommande(pompe, 2))
            commande.ajouter(LigneCommande(arc, 1))
            val martin = Client("Martin")
            martin.ajouter(commande)
            session.persist(martin)
        }
    }
}
    • Line 11: Like [BaseArticles], a [object] replaces the Java utility class;
    • lines 16–18: the six entities, declared by [managedClasses];
    • line 26: the function is an expression: the result of [JournalSql.sansJournal], to which the processing to be executed without a log (SQL) is passed;
    • lines 31–42: an object graph: three categories, their products, and the products’ labels;
    • lines 44–46: it is sufficient to persist the categories: thanks to cascading, Hibernate traverses the associations and persists all the entities it reaches, in the correct order (the categories before the products that reference them), populating the foreign keys and the association table;
    • lines 48–53: a customer, their order, and its two line items, persisted in a single operation.

    • the table [produits]: its foreign key [categorie_id] references the table [categories]. It is [NOT NULL] ([optional = false]). MySQL creates an index on each foreign key (row [KEY]). Unlike other ORM entries, Hibernate does not require cascade deletion in the database ([ON DELETE CASCADE]): this can be achieved using the [@OnDelete(action = OnDeleteAction.CASCADE)] annotation;
    • the association table has two columns—foreign keys to the two linked tables—which together form its primary key.

    package relations

import org.hibernate.LazyInitializationException
import org.hibernate.Session
import java.math.BigDecimal
import java.time.LocalDate

// relationships between entities: lazy loading, join fetch, entity graph, joins

// Results of projection queries
data class ProduitCategorie(val produit: String, val categorie: String)

data class MontantCommande(val id: Int, val client: String, val montant: BigDecimal)

data class StatistiquesCategorie(val categorie: String, val nombre: Long, val prixMoyen: Double)

fun main() {
    Boutique.creerSessionFactory().use { sessionFactory ->
         // 1 - Creating tables and an initial dataset, without a log
        Boutique.initialiser(sessionFactory)

         // 2 - A customer, their order, and its line items, added all at once
        println("--- ajout d'un client, d'une commande et de ses deux lignes")
        sessionFactory.inTransaction { session ->
            val velo = session.produit("vélo")
            val fleches = session.produit("flèches - lot de 6")
            val commande = Commande(LocalDate.of(2026, 10, 1))
            commande.ajouter(LigneCommande(velo, 1))
            commande.ajouter(LigneCommande(fleches, 3))
            val client = Client("Dupont")
            client.ajouter(commande)
            session.persist(client)
            println("client n° ${client.id}, commande n° ${commande.id}")
        }

         // 3 - lazy loading: relations are read on demand
        println("--- chargement paresseux")
        sessionFactory.inSession { session ->
            val commandes = session
                .createSelectionQuery("from Commande order by id", Commande::class.java)
                .resultList
            for (commande in commandes) {
                 // The customer and order lines are only read here, when they are first used
                println("commande n° ${commande.id} : client=${commande.client.nom}, " +
                        "${commande.lignes.size} ligne(s)")
            }
             // The property [client] contains a delegate: an object of a subclass of Client
            println("classe du client : ${commandes[0].client.javaClass.name}")
        }

         // 4 - An unloaded relation is no longer accessible once the session is closed
        println("--- après la fermeture de la session")
        val commandeDetachee = sessionFactory.fromSession { it.find(Commande::class.java, 1) }
        try {
            println("${commandeDetachee.lignes.size} ligne(s)")
        } catch (e: LazyInitializationException) {
            println("${e.javaClass.simpleName} : ${e.message}")
        }

         // 5 - join fetch: orders, their customers, their lines, and their products in a single query
        println("--- join fetch")
        sessionFactory.inSession { session ->
            val commandes = session.createSelectionQuery(
                """
                from Commande c
                join fetch c.client
                join fetch c.lignes l
                join fetch l.produit
                order by c.id""", Commande::class.java
            ).resultList
            for (commande in commandes) {
                println("commande n° ${commande.id} du ${commande.date} pour ${commande.client.nom}")
                for (ligne in commande.lignes) {
                    val produit = ligne.produit
                    println("  %d x %s à %.2f euros".format(ligne.quantite, produit.nom, produit.prix))
                }
            }
        }

         // 6 - an entity graph: what needs to be loaded with the entity, described outside the query
        println("--- graphe d'entités")
        val categorie = sessionFactory.fromSession { session ->
            val graphe = session.createEntityGraph(Categorie::class.java)
            graphe.addAttributeNodes(Categorie::produits.name)
            session.find(graphe, 2)
        }
         // The session is closed, but the products have been loaded
        println("${categorie.nom} : ${categorie.produits.joinToString(", ") { it.nom }}")

         // 7 - The many-to-many relationship in a single query
        println("--- les produits en promotion")
        sessionFactory.inSession { session ->
            session.createSelectionQuery(
                """
                select p.nom, p.categorie.nom from Produit p join p.etiquettes e
                where e.libelle = :libelle order by p.nom""", ProduitCategorie::class.java
            )
                .setParameter("libelle", "promo")
                .resultList
                .forEach { (produit, categorie) -> println("$produit ($categorie)") }
        }

         // 8 - a calculation across relationships, performed by SGBD
        println("--- montant des commandes")
        sessionFactory.inSession { session ->
            session.createSelectionQuery(
                """
                select c.id, c.client.nom, sum(l.quantite * l.produit.prix)
                from Commande c join c.lignes l
                group by c.id, c.client.nom order by c.id""", MontantCommande::class.java
            )
                .resultList
                .forEach { (id, client, montant) ->
                    println("commande n° %d (%s) : %.2f euros".format(id, client, montant))
                }
        }

         // 9 - a grouping: number of products and average price by category
        println("--- produits par catégorie")
        sessionFactory.inSession { session ->
            session.createSelectionQuery(
                """
                select p.categorie.nom, count(*), avg(p.prix) from Produit p
                group by p.categorie.nom order by p.categorie.nom""", StatistiquesCategorie::class.java
            )
                .resultList
                .forEach { (categorie, nombre, prixMoyen) ->
                    println("%s : %d produit(s), prix moyen %.2f euros".format(categorie, nombre, prixMoyen))
                }
        }
    }
}

// The product with a given name: a session extension function
fun Session.produit(nom: String): Produit =
    createSelectionQuery("from Produit where nom = :nom", Produit::class.java)
        .setParameter("nom", nom)
        .singleResult

    Comments:

    • Lines 11–15: The data classes that will receive the projection results. Their types correspond to those returned by SGBD: [Long] for [count], [Double] for [avg];
    • lines 135–138: the product with the given name, read by an extension function of the Hibernate interface [Session]: inside it, [createSelectionQuery] is called on the session itself ([this], implicit). It is called as a session method: [session.produit("vélo")] (line 25), where the Java code previously defined a static method [produit(session, "vélo")];
    • lines 24–33: a customer, their order, and its two lines are persisted with a single call to [persist]. SQL shows the order of insertions: first the customer, then the order—whose foreign key [client_id] receives the generated key from the customer (2)—and finally the lines, whose foreign key [commande_id] receives the key from the order. [inTransaction] receives a Kotlin lambda where Hibernate expects a Java functional interface ([Consumer<Session>]): this is the conversion SAM from Chapter 7;
    • lines 39–45: lazy loading. The query reads only the orders: the customer and the lines for each order are read only when the program uses them, via additional queries (two for the first order, two for the second). For the customer, Hibernate has placed a proxy in the [client] property—an object of a subclass of [Client] generated by Hibernate (using Byte Buddy)—which contains only the identifier and reads the client on the first call to an accessor ([commande.client.nom], i.e., [getNom()]). Line 48 shows this: the object’s class is [relations.Client$HibernateProxy]. This is why an entity must not be a final class, nor its accessors final methods: in Kotlin, where classes and members are final by default, it is the [allopen] plugin that makes them non-final. For the rows, the list is a Hibernate collection, loaded on first use ([size]);
    • Lines 53–57: The command is read by a session that is immediately closed ([fromSession], which returns the result of the lambda). These lines were not loaded, and once the session is closed, they can no longer be loaded: accessing the collection triggers a [LazyInitializationException], one of the most common exceptions in applications that use Hibernate. Nothing in the property’s [MutableList<LigneCommande>] type signals this risk to the Kotlin compiler: type safety ends where on-demand loading begins. You must load what you’ll need while the session is open;
    • lines 63–69: preloading via a query. [join fetch] instructs Hibernate to load, along with the orders, their customers, their lines, and the product of each line: a single query with joins. The output shows both orders and their lines. The join with the rows produces one SQL row per order line; Hibernate derives a single order for each ID: the rendered list does indeed contain two orders. The query text, spanning multiple lines, is a raw string;
    • lines 82–88: an “entity graph” (Jakarta Persistence) describes, outside of any query, the associations to be loaded with an entity: here, the products in the category, identified by the property reference [Categorie::produits.name] rather than by the string ["produits"]. [session.find(graphe, 2)] (Jakarta Persistence 3.2) reads category 2 along with its products in a single query (an outer join, [left join]). Once the session is closed, the products remain accessible. To load an association later, while the session is open, use [Hibernate.initialize(categorie.produits)]. Note the call to [addAttributeNodes] (plural) rather than [addAttributeNode]: the latter, which is generic, returns a *[AttributeNode<Y>]*, and Kotlin cannot infer the type *[Y]* when the result is not used (“cannot infer type for type parameter 'Y'”);
    • Lines 95–100: associations are used in queries: [join p.etiquettes e] traverses the many-to-many relationship (two joins, with the association table and the label table), and [p.categorie.nom] is translated into an implicit join with the category table. The label text is passed via a named parameter (the Java course wrote it as a literal in the query); each result is unpacked into the lambda’s parameters: [{ (produit, categorie) -> ... \}];
    • lines 108–114: a calculation involving two relations—the amount of each order—entirely performed by SGBD: joins, [sum] and [group by];
    • lines 123–128: a grouping. [group by p.categorie.nom] groups products by category name; for each group, the number of products ([count], of type [Long]) and the average price ([avg], of type [Double]) are calculated by SGBD. The category [plongée], which has no product, does not appear: the join with the category table is an inner join ([join]).

    11.8.3. The N+1 Query Problem

    The lazy loading in the example illustrates a problem that affects any user of a ORM, known as the “N+1 queries” problem: one query to read the N orders, then one query per order to read its customer (and another for its line items). With a thousand orders, this results in a thousand and one round trips to the server, when a single one would have sufficed. The problem is all the more insidious because it’s invisible in the code: [commande.client.nom] doesn’t look like a query, and Kotlin’s property syntax hides it even better than the Java call [getClient().getNom()]. The solutions are those shown in the example: [join fetch], an entity graph, or better yet, a projection onto a data class that retrieves only the necessary data. Hibernate also offers batch loading ([@BatchSize(size = 20)] applied to a collection, or to the referenced entity class, in this case [Client]), which, for example, retrieves the customers for twenty orders in a single query. The log SQL helps identify the problem: the same query being repeated numerous times.

    11.9. Changes to the database schema

    11.9.1. The Problem

    Until now, tables were created by Hibernate after being deleted. This is impossible for a live application: its database contains data that must be preserved when the model evolves (a new column, a new table). It must be possible to migrate the database from one schema version to the next, in a safe and reproducible manner, both on the developer’s machine and on the production server. This is referred to as schema migration.

    Hibernate does not support schema migrations: it can create a schema, validate it, and make limited updates to it. The standard practice, as described in JVM (in both Java and Kotlin), is to delegate migrations to versioned SQL scripts, applied by a dedicated tool—most commonly Flyway or Liquibase—and to have Hibernate verify that the resulting schema matches the entities.

    11.9.2. Schema Management by Hibernate

    The [hibernate.hbm2ddl.auto] property (or the [schemaToolingAction] method in the configuration, which is used by the program below) specifies what Hibernate should do with the schema when creating the [SessionFactory]:

    Value
    Constant [Action]
    Effect
    [none]
    [NONE]
    none (default value)
    [create-only]
    [CREATE_ONLY]
    table creation
    [create]
    [CREATE]
    Deleting and then creating tables
    [create-drop]
    [CREATE_DROP]
    such as [create], and deletion of tables upon closing [SessionFactory]: for testing
    [drop]
    [DROP]
    Delete the tables
    [validate]
    [VALIDATE]
    Check that the tables and columns of the entities exist, with compatible types; throw an exception otherwise
    [update]
    [UPDATE]
    Create any missing tables and columns

    Jakarta Persistence defines a related property, [jakarta.persistence.schema-generation.database.action], with the values [none], [create], [drop-and-create], and [drop]. The same actions are available programmatically, as we did with [SchemaManager] from [SessionFactory] ([create], [drop], [validate], [truncate]).

    The [update] option is tempting: Hibernate compares the entities to the database schema and adds what’s missing. It has limitations that make it unsuitable for a production application:

    • it only adds: it never deletes a column or table that has become unnecessary, does not modify the type or length of an existing column, and cannot rename (renaming a property creates a new empty column, while the old one remains with its data);
    • it cannot transform data (fill a new required column, split a column into two);
    • what it does depends on the state of the database it encounters: it is impossible to know in advance which commands will be executed, or in what order, and no record of this is kept.

    We therefore reserve [create], [create-drop], and [update] for development and testing, and we use [validate] (or [none]) in production, with the schema managed by scripts.

    11.9.3. Versioned SQL scripts

    The principle behind script-based migrations is simple:

    • each schema change is described by a script named SQL, numbered sequentially: [V1__creation_clients.sql], [V2__ajout_telephone.sql]... Once a script has been applied to a database, it is never modified again: any correction is the subject of a new script;
    • the database contains a history table that lists the versions that have been applied to it;
    • When the application starts (or during deployment), a tool compares the available scripts with the history and applies, in order, those that have not yet been applied.

    The scripts are part of the application’s source code: they are stored and managed along with the rest of the code (in a Git repository, for example). To understand how this works, the [clients] subproject implements a small versioned script runner, modeled after Flyway; we will then introduce Flyway itself.

    11.9.4. The [clients] subproject

    The [clients] subproject uses the [hbclients] base project. It has two programs: [clients.MainKt], which runs by default, and [clients.GenerationScriptKt], which is specified as needed by the [main] property, as in the previous chapters. Its [build.gradle.kts] is the same as that of the [relations] subproject, with one exception:

     // or the one specified by the property [main]: gradlew -q :clients:run -Pmain=clients.GenerationScriptKt
    mainClass = providers.gradleProperty("main").orElse("clients.MainKt")
}

import jakarta.persistence.Column
import jakarta.persistence.Entity
import jakarta.persistence.GeneratedValue
import jakarta.persistence.GenerationType
import jakarta.persistence.Id
import jakarta.persistence.Table

// a client
@Entity
@Table(name = "clients")
class Client(
    @Column(nullable = false, length = 50)
    var nom: String,
    @Column(nullable = false, length = 100)
    var email: String,
     // version 2: the phone number, optional (type `String?` and a column that accepts `NULL`)
    @Column(length = 20)
    var telephone: String? = null,
) {
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    var id: Int? = null
        protected set

    override fun toString() = "[$id, $nom, $email, ${telephone ?: "pas de téléphone"}]"
}

    In the first version of the application, the customer does not have a phone number: lines 18–20 do not yet exist. We will add them in the second version. The phone number is optional, which Kotlin expresses using the nullable type [String?] and the default value [null] (so we can create a customer without a phone number: [Client("Durand", "durand@example.com")]). Hibernate, however, does not recognize Kotlin types: it is the absence of ***[nullable = false] in *[@Column] that makes the column optional (conversely, a non-nullable Kotlin [String] only produces a [NOT NULL] column if explicitly requested, as is the case with [nom] and [email]). The [toString] function (line 27) uses the Elvis operator to display the absence of a phone number.

    The scripts are located in the [src/main/resources/db/migration] folder of the subproject, which Gradle copies to the classpath (into the [build/resources/main] folder). These are the scripts from the Java course: a script named SQL is not dependent on the application’s programming language. The first one creates the table:

    package clients

import java.nio.file.Path
import java.sql.Connection
import java.sql.DriverManager
import java.sql.SQLException
import kotlin.io.path.listDirectoryEntries
import kotlin.io.path.name
import kotlin.io.path.readLines

// A small script runner for versioned SQL scripts, modeled after Flyway: the scripts
// [db/migration/V<version>__<description>.sql] are applied only once, in version order,
//, and the table [historique_migrations] in the database records which ones have been applied
class Migrations(
    private val url: String,
    private val utilisateur: String,
    private val motDePasse: String,
) {
     // a migration script
    data class Script(val version: Int, val description: String, val chemin: Path) {
        override fun toString() = "V$version ($description)"
    }

    private companion object {
         // the name of a script: V1__creation_clients.sql
        val NOM = Regex("""V(\d+)__(\w+)\.sql""")

         // the history table
        const val CREATION_HISTORIQUE = """
            create table if not exists historique_migrations (
                version integer not null primary key,
                description varchar(100) not null,
                date_application datetime not null default current_timestamp
            ) engine=InnoDB"""
    }

     // a database connection
    private fun connexion(): Connection = DriverManager.getConnection(url, utilisateur, motDePasse)

     // scripts in the [db/migration] folder in the classpath, sorted by version
    fun scripts(): List<Script> {
        val dossier = Migrations::class.java.getResource("/db/migration") ?: return emptyList()
        return Path.of(dossier.toURI()).listDirectoryEntries()
            .mapNotNull { fichier ->
                 // files whose names do not follow the convention are ignored (null)
                NOM.matchEntire(fichier.name)?.destructured?.let { (version, description) ->
                    Script(version.toInt(), description.replace('_', ' '), fichier)
                }
            }
            .sortedBy { it.version }
    }

     // versions already applied to the database (the history table is created if necessary)
    fun versionsAppliquees(): Set<Int> = connexion().use { cnx ->
        cnx.createStatement().use { ordre ->
            ordre.execute(CREATION_HISTORIQUE)
            ordre.executeQuery("select version from historique_migrations").use { lignes ->
                sortedSetOf<Int>().apply {
                    while (lignes.next()) add(lignes.getInt(1))
                }
            }
        }
    }

     // scripts that still need to be applied
    fun enAttente(): List<Script> {
        val appliquees = versionsAppliquees()
        return scripts().filter { it.version !in applied }
    }

     // Apply pending scripts, up to and including version [cible]; mark the scripts as applied
    fun appliquer(cible: Int = Int.MAX_VALUE): List<Script> =
        enAttente().takeWhile { it.version <= cible }.onEach { appliquer(it) }

     // Apply a script and add its version to the history within a transaction
    private fun appliquer(script: Script) {
         // the script's commands, separated by semicolons, without comment lines
        val ordres = script.chemin.readLines()
            .filterNot { it.trim().startsWith("--") }
            .joinToString("\n")
            .split(";")
            .filter { it.isNotBlank() }
        connexion().use { cnx ->
            cnx.autoCommit = false
            try {
                cnx.createStatement().use { ordre -> ordres.forEach { ordre.execute(it) } }
                cnx.prepareStatement("insert into historique_migrations(version, description) values (?, ?)")
                    .use { historique ->
                        historique.setInt(1, script.version)
                        historique.setString(2, script.description)
                        historique.executeUpdate()
                    }
                cnx.commit()
            } catch (e: SQLException) {
                 // Warning: under MySQL, a schema modification command cannot be rolled back
                cnx.rollback()
                throw e
            }
        }
    }
}
    • lines 14–17: the database is described by the private properties of the primary constructor;
    • lines 20–21: a script is described by a nested data class, [Migrations.Script]: its version, description, and path; its [toString] method is overridden for display;
    • lines 24–34: the class constants, in a private companion object. Line 26: a script’s name follows the Flyway convention: [V]—the version number, two underscores, and a description. The regular expression is written as a raw string, where the backslash does not need to be doubled (["""V(\d+)__(\w+)\.sql"""]; in Java: ["V(\\d+)__(\\w+)\\.sql"]). The history table (one row per applied version, with its description and the date it was applied) is created by a command written as a raw string, a constant [const val];
    • lines 41–50: the list of scripts. [getResource("/db/migration")] returns the URL from the directory in the classpath, or [null] if it does not exist: the Elvis operator then immediately returns an empty list ([?: return emptyList()]). The directory is listed by the [listDirectoryEntries] extension function of [kotlin.io.path] (Chapter 5). Each file is checked against the regular expression by [matchEntire], which returns [null] if the name does not match: [mapNotNull] filters out these files, and the expression’s groups are retrieved via destructuring ([destructured], Chapter 5). This code assumes that the directory is a real directory (which is the case when the program is run by Gradle from the [build/resources/main] directory); Flyway can also read scripts from a [.jar] archive. The scripts are sorted by version number ([sortedBy]): alphabetical sorting would place [V10] before [V2];
    • Lines 54–59: The versions that have already been applied, retrieved from the history table, which is created as needed ([create table if not exists]). The three JDBC resources (connection, order, results) are closed by three nested [use] resources. The function returns a sorted set ([sortedSetOf], a Java [TreeSet]), populated by [apply];
    • lines 66–68: the remaining scripts to be applied: the [!in] operator checks for the absence of a version in the set;
    • lines 72–73: application of the pending scripts, up to a given version (all by default: [cible: Int = Int.MAX_VALUE]). [takeWhile] retains the scripts as long as their version does not exceed the target; [onEach] applies each of them and returns the list itself: the function fits into a single expression, whereas Java would have written a loop using [break];
    • lines 76–97: applying a script: its commands (comment lines removed by [filterNot], the text split at semicolons), then adding its version to the history table, within a transaction ([cnx.autoCommit = false], the Kotlin property corresponding to [setAutoCommit]). One caveat, noted in the comment on line 95: under MySQL, a schema modification command ([CREATE TABLE], [ALTER TABLE]) implicitly commits the current transaction and cannot be rolled back. If an error occurs in the middle of a script, the database may remain in an intermediate state. This is why it is advisable to use short scripts, each performing a single operation.

    Note that no function in the class declares the exceptions it may throw: the Java version had to specify [throws SQLException, IOException, URISyntaxException] on most of its methods, as well as on the [main] method that calls them. Kotlin does not have controlled exceptions (Chapter 3): a [SQLException] simply propagates up to whoever wants to handle it.

    package clients

import jakarta.persistence.PersistenceException
import org.hibernate.cfg.AvailableSettings
import org.hibernate.jpa.HibernatePersistenceConfiguration
import org.hibernate.tool.schema.Action

// the customer database; MySQL creates it if it does not exist
const val URL = "jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/hbclients?createDatabaseIfNotExist=true"

fun main(args: Array<String>) {
     // Target version: the latest by default, or the one passed as an argument
    val cible = args.firstOrNull()?.toInt() ?: Int.MAX_VALUE

     // the status of the migrations
    val migrations = Migrations(URL, "root", "")
    println("versions appliquées : ${migrations.versionsAppliquees()}")
    println("migrations en attente : ${migrations.enAttente()}")

     // Applies pending migrations
    for (script in migrations.appliquer(cible)) {
        println("migration appliquée : $script")
    }

     // Hibernate checks that the database schema matches the entities (validates)
    try {
        HibernatePersistenceConfiguration("clients")
            .managedClass(Client::class.java)
            .jdbcUrl(URL)
            .jdbcCredentials("root", "")
            .property(AvailableSettings.FORMAT_SQL, true)
            .schemaToolingAction(Action.VALIDATE)
            .createEntityManagerFactory()
            .use { sessionFactory ->
                println("le schéma de la base est conforme aux entités")
                 // the new column is usable
                sessionFactory.inTransaction { session ->
                    session.persist(Client("Dupont", "dupont@example.com", "01 23 45 67 89"))
                }
                sessionFactory.inSession { session ->
                    session.createSelectionQuery("from Client", Client::class.java)
                        .resultList
                        .forEach(::println)
                }
            }
    } catch (e: PersistenceException) {
         // The validation error is the cause of the exception
        val cause = e.cause ?: e
        println("${cause.javaClass.simpleName} : ${cause.message}")
    }
}
    • line 9: the database’s URL, a top-level constant in the [clients] package, which the second program will also use;
    • line 13: You can specify, as an argument, the version up to which to apply the migrations; by default, all are applied. [args.firstOrNull()?.toInt() ?: Int.MAX_VALUE] combines the safe call and the Elvis operator;
    • lines 16–22: the status of the migrations, followed by their application;
    • lines 27–34: [SessionFactory] is created with the action [VALIDATE]: Hibernate verifies that the database schema matches the entity [Client]. If this is not the case, the creation of [SessionFactory] fails with a [PersistenceException], the cause of which is the validation error (lines 46–49). [e.cause ?: e] captures the cause, or the exception itself if it has none;
    • lines 37–43: the new column is used.

    11.9.5. Generating Scripts with Hibernate

    The SQL scripts are written by hand. However, Hibernate can help write them: it can generate—without executing it—the script to create the schema, or, by comparing the entities to an existing database, the script to update it. This is what the program [GenerationScript.kt] does:

    package clients

import org.hibernate.cfg.AvailableSettings
import org.hibernate.jpa.HibernatePersistenceConfiguration
import java.io.StringWriter

// Hibernate generates the script SQL, which creates or updates the database schema
fun main(args: Array<String>) {
     // The action: create (default) or update
    val action = args.firstOrNull() ?: "create"
    val script = StringWriter()
     // A SessionFactory that writes the script without executing it; it is created solely for this purpose:
     // it is immediately closed
    HibernatePersistenceConfiguration("clients")
        .managedClass(Client::class.java)
        .jdbcUrl(URL)
        .jdbcCredentials("root", "")
        .property(AvailableSettings.JAKARTA_HBM2DDL_SCRIPTS_ACTION, action)
        .property(AvailableSettings.JAKARTA_HBM2DDL_SCRIPTS_CREATE_TARGET, script)
        .property(AvailableSettings.HBM2DDL_DELIMITER, ";")
        .property(AvailableSettings.FORMAT_SQL, true)
        .createEntityManagerFactory()
        .close()
     // the script, without removing the 4 spaces from its lines
    script.toString().trim().lines()
        .map { it.removePrefix("    ").trimEnd() }
        .forEach(::println)
}
    • line 10: the action, passed as an argument: [create] or [update];
    • lines 14–23: [SessionFactory] is created solely to generate the script: it is closed immediately after creation, without even being stored in a variable (the Java course declared it in a [try] statement with resources, using the anonymous Java variable [_] from Java 22);
    • lines 18–21: the script generation properties, already encountered in the subproject [modele]. This time, Hibernate connects to the database: for the action [update], it needs to know its schema;
    • lines 25–27: the script, with the 4-space indentation removed from its lines by [removePrefix], which only removes the prefix if it is present.

    Note that the two programs in the subproject each have a high-level [main] function in the same package: this is permitted for the [main] function, as each is compiled into its own file class ([clients.MainKt], [clients.GenerationScriptKt]).
