    11.9.7. Flyway

    Flyway is the most widely used migration tool for JVM (Spring Boot runs it automatically when an application starts if it is present in the classpath). It works exactly according to the same principle as our executor, but is more comprehensive: [V<version>__<description>.sql] scripts are searched for by default in the [db/migration] folder of the classpath, the [flyway_schema_history] history table is used, and pending scripts are applied in version order. In particular, it adds a checksum for each script, which detects changes to a script that has already been applied; “repeatable” scripts ([R__description.sql], reapplied with each change, for views for example); migrations written in the application’s language (Java or Kotlin classes); a lock that prevents two instances of the application from migrating the database at the same time, and a Gradle plugin (tasks [flywayMigrate], [flywayInfo]).

    To use it in the [clients] subproject, simply add the dependencies [org.flywaydb:flyway-core] and [org.flywaydb:flyway-mysql] (in their latest versions) to [build.gradle.kts], keep both scripts as is—since they already follow its convention—and replace the use of the [Migrations] class with a single line: [Flyway.configure().dataSource(URL, "root", "").load().migrate()].

    Liquibase, the other commonly used tool, describes schema changes in files named XML, YAML, or SQL (the “changelogs”), and can generate the SQL specific to each SGBD. In both cases, Hibernate is configured with [validate] or [none], and no longer modifies the schema.

    11.10. Hibernate and Virtual Threads

    A database query is an I/O operation: while the server is processing the request, the waiting thread does nothing. Chapters 8 and 9 presented two ways to avoid wasting threads during these waits: JDK virtual threads and Kotlin coroutines. Hibernate’s API, like the JDBC it uses, is blocking: [getResultList] (the [resultList] property in Kotlin) does not yield control until the lines have been read. With virtual threads, this is no longer a drawback: a virtual thread blocked on I/O frees up the system thread that was executing it, and you can create thousands of them. So you write ordinary blocking code, executed by virtual threads. With coroutines, we similarly entrust this blocking code to a dispatcher designed for I/O, [Dispatchers.IO] (Chapter 9), using [withContext]: the coroutine waiting for the result is suspended, without blocking its thread.

    One rule must be followed in both cases: a session is not thread-safe. It is never shared among multiple threads or multiple coroutines: each thread, each task, and each coroutine opens its own session with [SessionFactory], which is itself shared. With coroutines, this rule requires special attention: a coroutine may resume execution after a suspension on a different thread than the one where it started; a session opened before a suspended call and used after it would therefore switch threads. The simplest approach is to open and close the session within the [withContext] block, which contains no suspension points. Hibernate does not always detect concurrent use of the same session; the resulting errors are unpredictable.

    package asynchrone

import articles.Article
import articles.BaseArticles
import jakarta.persistence.QueryTimeoutException
import java.math.BigDecimal
import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture
import java.util.concurrent.Executors
import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers
import kotlinx.coroutines.async
import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking
import kotlinx.coroutines.withContext
import org.hibernate.SessionFactory

// Hibernate (a blocking API) with virtual threads, then with coroutines
fun main() {
    BaseArticles.creerSessionFactory().use { sessionFactory ->
         // the table [articles] is recreated with its six entries
        BaseArticles.initialiser(sessionFactory)

         // 1 - Two queries executed simultaneously by two virtual threads, each with its own session
        println("--- deux requêtes en parallèle")
        Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().use { executeur ->
            val petitsPrix = executeur.submit<List<Article>> {
                sessionFactory.fromSession { s ->
                    s.createSelectionQuery("from Article where prix < 200 order by prix", Article::class.java)
                        .resultList
                }
            }
            val hql = "select count(*) from Article where stockActuel < stockMinimum"
            val enRupture = executeur.submit<Long> {
                sessionFactory.fromSession { s ->
                    s.createSelectionQuery(hql, Long::class.java).singleResult
                }
            }
             // get() waits for each task to complete
            petitsPrix.get().forEach { println(it) }
            println("${enRupture.get()} article(s) en rupture")
        }

         // 2 - a transaction executed by a virtual thread, followed by processing of its result
        println("--- CompletableFuture")
        Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().use { executeur ->
            val traitement = CompletableFuture
                .supplyAsync({
                    sessionFactory.fromTransaction { session ->
                        session.createSelectionQuery("from Article where nom = 'arc'", Article::class.java)
                            .singleResult
                            .apply { prix = BigDecimal.valueOf(550) }
                    }
                }, executeur)
                .thenAccept { arc -> println("nouveau prix de l'arc : ${arc.prix}") }
            traitement.join()
        }

         // 3 - coroutines: each executes a suspension function that opens its own session
        println("--- coroutines")
        runBlocking {
             // two child coroutines of runBlocking, executed simultaneously
            val petits = async {
                compter(sessionFactory, "select count(*) from Article where prix < 200")
            }
            val chers = async {
                compter(sessionFactory, "select count(*) from Article where prix >= 200")
            }
             // `await()` suspends the main coroutine until each child coroutine returns
            println("${petits.await()} article(s) à moins de 200 euros")
            println("${chers.await()} article(s) à 200 euros ou plus")
        }

         // 4 - a stream: entities are processed as they are read
        println("--- getResultStream")
        sessionFactory.inSession { session ->
            session.createSelectionQuery("from Article where prix >= 300", Article::class.java)
                .resultStream
                .use { articles -> articles.forEach { println("lu : ${it.nom}") } }
        }

         // 5 - A query that takes too long is terminated after the specified timeout (in seconds)
        println("--- délai dépassé")
        try {
            sessionFactory.inSession { session ->
                session.createNativeQuery("select sleep(5)", Int::class.java)
                    .setTimeout(1)
                    .singleResult
            }
        } catch (e: QueryTimeoutException) {
            println("${e::class.simpleName} : ${e.message}")
        }
    }
}

// A counting request executed in a coroutine-specific session; the blocking work is
// delegated to the [IO] dispatcher: the calling coroutine is suspended, but its thread is not blocked
suspend fun compter(sessionFactory: SessionFactory, hql: String): Long =
    withContext(Dispatchers.IO) {
        sessionFactory.fromSession { session ->
            session.createSelectionQuery(hql, Long::class.java).singleResult
        }
    }

    Comments:

    • line 23: an executor that creates a virtual thread per task (Chapter 8). A [ExecutorService] is [AutoCloseable]: the function [use] closes it at the end of the block, and its closure waits for all tasks to finish;
    • Lines 24–33: Two tasks submitted to the executor. Each opens its own session ([fromSession]) and executes a query; both queries run simultaneously, on two connections from the pool. Their order in the log (lines 3–9 of the results) may therefore vary from one execution to another. The result type is specified in [submit] ([submit<List<Article>>]): otherwise, the lambda might be interpreted as a [Runnable]—which returns nothing—rather than as a [Callable];
    • Line 33: the type of the result of the count query. [Long::class.java] here refers to the Java primitive type [long]; Hibernate accepts it and returns the value as a [java.lang.Long], which Kotlin treats as a [Long];
    • lines 36–38: [get()] waits for each task to complete and returns its result (lines 10–13);
    • lines 44–53: a [CompletableFuture] (Chapter 9) whose first step—a complete transaction—is executed by a virtual thread ([supplyAsync(..., executeur)]), and the second step displays its result. The function [apply] modifies the read record and returns it: this is the value of the lambda, and thus the result of the transaction. The record returned by the transaction is detached (its session is closed): we can read its properties but not load its associations;
    • lines 58–68: the same idea using coroutines. [runBlocking] creates a main coroutine; [async] launches two child coroutines, which call the suspension function [compter]. Both requests run simultaneously (lines 30–35), and [await] suspends the main coroutine until each one returns (lines 36–37);
    • lines 95–96: the suspension function delegates the blocking work to the [Dispatchers.IO] dispatcher, whose threads are designed to wait for I/O operations. The session is opened and closed by [fromSession] within the [withContext] block: it is used by only one coroutine, and on a single thread. This is the approach to use when calling Hibernate from suspended code. One could also use a dispatcher built on virtual threads ([Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().asCoroutineDispatcher()], Chapter 9);
    • lines 73–76: the property [resultStream] (the method [getResultStream]) returns a Java stream: entities are processed as they are read, without forming a list (lines 42–44). A stream is [AutoCloseable]: [use] closes it, which releases the cursor JDBC. It could also be converted to a Kotlin sequence ([asSequence()], Chapter 5). This is useful for processing a large number of lines. With MySQL, note that by default the driver reads all lines of the result before returning the first one; for truly progressive reading, you must instruct it to use a cursor (parameter [useCursorFetch=true] of URL and batch size set by [setFetchSize]);
    • Lines 83–87: A maximum execution time, in seconds, set by [setTimeout]. The query (a native SQL query, which we’ll discuss later) takes five seconds; after one second, the JDBC driver interrupts it, and Hibernate launches a [QueryTimeoutException] (lines 46–48).

    The duration of the last request warrants a note. In Chapter 9, we canceled coroutines ([job.cancel()], [withTimeout]) and tasks ([Future.cancel]). These cancellations would have no effect on the request here: canceling a coroutine is cooperative, and a coroutine blocked in the driver JDBC does not check whether it has been canceled; as for interrupting a thread blocked in the driver, it does not interrupt the request currently in progress on the server. A [withTimeout(1000) { compter(...) }] would indeed launch a [TimeoutCancellationException]... but only once the request is complete, after five seconds: the [withContext] block of [compter] does not yield control until it has finished its blocking operation. To limit the duration of a request, you must therefore address the JDBC driver via [setTimeout].

    For applications that require a truly non-blocking API, there is Hibernate Reactive, a variant of Hibernate that relies on reactive drivers (those from Vert.x) rather than JDBC, and whose methods return [CompletionStage] or objects from the Mutiny library; A [CompletionStage] is expected in a coroutine with the [await] extension function from kotlinx-coroutines. Virtual threads and the [Dispatchers.IO] dispatcher eliminate this complexity in most cases: this is the approach taken in this course.

    11.11. Transactions and Concurrency

    11.11.1. Transactions

    Chapter 10 introduced transactions: a set of operations that either all succeed or all fail. With Hibernate:

    • every write operation is performed within a transaction, opened by [session.beginTransaction()] and closed by [commit] or [rollback]. The methods [inTransaction] and [fromTransaction] of [SessionFactory] handle this for us: they commit the transaction if the lambda completes normally, and roll it back if it throws an exception, which is then rethrown;
    • all commands sent during the transaction (immediate commands via [INSERT], explicit synchronizations via [flush], and synchronization via [commit]) are either committed or rolled back together;
    • An error from SGBD is propagated as a Hibernate exception, derived from [JDBCException], which encapsulates the driver’s [SQLException]: [ConstraintViolationException] for a constraint violation (primary key, uniqueness, foreign key, [NOT NULL]), [SQLGrammarException] for an error in the order SQL, and so on. These are uncaught exceptions, in both Java and Kotlin (which, as a reminder, does not have caught exceptions: Chapter 3); we only catch those that we know how to handle.

    package transactions

import articles.Article
import articles.BaseArticles
import java.math.BigDecimal
import org.hibernate.SessionFactory
import org.hibernate.exception.ConstraintViolationException

// the two ways to manage a transaction: inTransaction, and a transaction managed by the code
fun main() {
    BaseArticles.creerSessionFactory().use { sessionFactory ->
         // The table [articles] is recreated with its six records
        BaseArticles.initialiser(sessionFactory)

         // 1 - inTransaction: validation if everything succeeds, rollback in case of an exception
        println("--- deux ajouts dont le second viole l'unicité du nom")
        try {
            sessionFactory.inTransaction { session ->
                session.persist(Article("raquette", BigDecimal.valueOf(80), 5, 2))
                session.persist(Article("vélo", BigDecimal.valueOf(450), 3, 1))
            }
        } catch (e: ConstraintViolationException) {
            println("${e::class.simpleName} : contrainte [${e.constraintName}] violée")
        }
        afficher(sessionFactory, "raquette")

         // 2 - A transaction managed by the code: multiple entries, validated or canceled together
        println("--- transaction annulée")
        sessionFactory.openSession().use { session ->
            val transaction = session.beginTransaction()
            try {
                 // sale of two bicycles: the UPDATE is sent via flush
                val velo = session
                    .createSelectionQuery("from Article where nom = 'vélo'", Article::class.java)
                    .singleResult
                velo.stockActuel -= 2
                session.flush()
                 // Adding an item with a name that already exists: error
                session.persist(Article("pompe", BigDecimal.valueOf(12), 5, 1))
                 // Validation of the entire set (this cannot be done here)
                transaction.commit()
            } catch (e: ConstraintViolationException) {
                println("${e::class.simpleName} : ${e.sqlException.message}")
                 // All operations in the transaction were canceled
                transaction.rollback()
            }
        }
         // The sale of the bicycles has been canceled
        afficher(sessionFactory, "vélo")
    }
}

// Displaying an item read from the database, with a new session
fun afficher(sessionFactory: SessionFactory, nom: String) {
    val article = sessionFactory.fromSession { session ->
        session.createSelectionQuery("from Article where nom = :nom", Article::class.java)
            .setParameter("nom", nom)
            .singleResultOrNull
    }
    println("article [$nom] dans la base : ${article ?: "absent"}")
}

    Comments:

    • Lines 18–20: Two items are added to a transaction managed by [inTransaction]; the second item has the same name as an existing item. Both [INSERT] processes are executed immediately (lines 4–15); the second violates the uniqueness constraint on the [nom] column: MySQL rejects it (line 16), [persist] launches a [ConstraintViolationException], [inTransaction] rolls back the transaction (line 17) and rethrows the exception;
    • lines 22–23: the exception is caught; the [constraintName] property (the [getConstraintName] method) returns the name of the violated constraint (line 18). This demonstrates the value of having named the constraint;
    • line 25: the racket, which had been successfully inserted, is not in the database (line 23): rolling back the transaction deleted it;
    • Lines 29–45: A transaction managed by the code, in a session opened by [openSession] and closed by [use] ([Session] is [AutoCloseable]). Two bicycles are sold ([velo.stockActuel -= 2]: the operator [-=] is applied to a property [var] just as it is to a variable), and the change is sent to SGBD via an explicit [flush] (lines 29–36); then an item is added whose name already exists: the insertion fails (line 43);
    • line 41: the commit is never reached;
    • lines 42–45: in the [catch], the transaction is rolled back (line 45 of the results). The [sqlException] property returns the original exception from the JDBC driver, and its message is that of MySQL (line 44);
    • line 49: the sale of bicycles, although sent to SGBD by [flush], was canceled: the bicycle inventory is still 10 (line 50);
    • lines 54–60: a function that re-reads a record with a new session to view the actual state of the database rather than the entities from the current working session. The property [singleResultOrNull] sets [null] if the query finds nothing; the Elvis operator ([?:]) then displays “absent.”

    After an exception, a session should no longer be used: its persistence context may contain entities in a state that is inconsistent with the database. We roll back the transaction, close the session, and start over if necessary with a new session. This is what [inTransaction] does, and what our code does when exiting the [use] block, which closes the session.

    The transaction isolation level is that of the JDBC connection: [REPEATABLE_READ], the default value for MySQL, as shown in the first example. You can change this for the entire [SessionFactory] using the [jdbcTransactionIsolation] method in the configuration.

    11.11.2. Optimistic Concurrency

    Two users are reading the same item, which has a stock of 10. The first user sells one item and updates the stock to 9. The second user, who read the stock value before this update, sells three items and updates the stock to 7: the first user’s sale is lost. This is the problem of lost updates.

    One solution would be to lock the row for the entire duration of each user’s operation (“pessimistic” concurrency): this blocks other users, sometimes for a long time. With Hibernate, optimistic concurrency is generally preferred: nothing is locked, but a check is performed at the time of saving to ensure that the row has not been modified since it was read. The standard way to do this is to add a version number to the entity—a property annotated with [@Version]. Hibernate increments this number each time the row is modified, and adds the condition “the version still has the value read” to the [WHERE] clause via the commands [UPDATE] and [DELETE]. If the transaction does not modify any rows, it means another user has already accessed the data: Hibernate executes a [OptimisticLockException].

    The subproject [concurrence] uses its own database, [hbconcurrence], and its own entity, [Article], stripped down to the essentials:

    // an item whose changes are tracked by a version number
@Entity
@Table(name = "articles")
class Article(
    @Column(nullable = false, length = 30)
    var nom: String,
    var stockActuel: Int,
) {
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    var id: Int? = null
        protected set

     // the version number: incremented by Hibernate each time the row is modified
    @Version
    var version: Int = 0
        protected set
}
    • lines 15–17: the version number, of the form [Int] (you can also use [Long], or a date in the form [Instant]). The application never modifies this itself: its modifier is protected ([protected set]), just like that of the identifier; Hibernate, which accesses the field directly, is not affected by this. The initial value [0] is that of an article created by the application; for an article read from the database, the parameterless constructor added by the plugin [jpa] does not perform this initialization (as we have seen), but Hibernate immediately assigns the read value to the property.

    package concurrence

import jakarta.persistence.OptimisticLockException
import org.hibernate.cfg.AvailableSettings
import org.hibernate.jpa.HibernatePersistenceConfiguration
import outils.JournalSql

// optimistic concurrency: two users edit the same article
fun main() {
    HibernatePersistenceConfiguration("concurrence")
        .managedClass(Article::class.java)
        .jdbcUrl("jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/hbconcurrence?createDatabaseIfNotExist=true")
        .jdbcCredentials("root", "")
        .property(AvailableSettings.FORMAT_SQL, true)
        .createEntityManagerFactory()
        .use { sessionFactory ->
             // the table [articles] is recreated with a single article, without a log
            JournalSql.sansJournal {
                sessionFactory.schemaManager.drop(false)
                sessionFactory.schemaManager.create(false)
                sessionFactory.inTransaction { session -> session.persist(Article("vélo", 10)) }
            }

             // Two users, two sessions: each reads the same item
            sessionFactory.openSession().use { session1 ->
                sessionFactory.openSession().use { session2 ->
                    println("--- les deux utilisateurs lisent le vélo")
                    val velo1 = session1.find(Article::class.java, 1)
                    val velo2 = session2.find(Article::class.java, 1)

                     // User 1 sells 1 bike
                    println("--- l'utilisateur 1 vend 1 vélo")
                    val transaction1 = session1.beginTransaction()
                    velo1.stockActuel -= 1
                    transaction1.commit()
                    println("stock enregistré par l'utilisateur 1 : ${velo1.etat()}")

                     // User 2 sells 3 bicycles based on outdated data (stock = 10, version 0)
                    println("--- l'utilisateur 2 vend 3 vélos")
                    val transaction2 = session2.beginTransaction()
                    velo2.stockActuel -= 3
                    try {
                        session2.flush()
                        transaction2.commit()
                    } catch (e: OptimisticLockException) {
                        println("${e::class.simpleName} : ${e.message}")
                        transaction2.rollback()
                    }
                }
            }

             // Solution: User 2 reloads the item in a new session and starts over
            println("--- l'utilisateur 2 relit le vélo et recommence")
            sessionFactory.inTransaction { session ->
                val velo = session.find(Article::class.java, 1)
                println("stock relu : ${velo.etat()}")
                velo.stockActuel -= 3
                session.flush()
                println("stock enregistré par l'utilisateur 2 : ${velo.etat()}")
            }
        }
}

// An item’s status for display: an extension function
fun Article.etat() = "$stockActuel (version $version)"

    Comments:

    • lines 10–15: the Hibernate configuration for the [hbconcurrence] database and its single entity;
    • lines 18–21: the table is recreated with a single item, the bicycle, version 0. The function [sansJournal] from the library [outils] receives the action to be executed in the form of a lambda, written without parentheses since it is its only parameter (Chapter 7);
    • lines 28–29: Each user reads the bicycle in their own session; the two sessions are opened by two nested [use] functions and closed in the reverse order of their opening. The [version] column is read along with the others (lines 3–10);
    • lines 33–35: the [UPDATE] order from the first user (lines 13–20) writes the new version (1) and contains the condition [version=?] with the read version (0). The row is modified; the entity’s [version] property is set to 1 (line 22);
    • lines 41–44: the second user’s request contains the same condition, with the version they read, 0, whereas the version of the row in the database is now 1. No rows are modified, and Hibernate throws a [OptimisticLockException] (line 33). We explicitly synchronize the session ([flush]) before the [commit] to trigger this exception as-is; if it were raised during the [commit], it would be encapsulated within a [RollbackException];
    • Lines 54–59: The resolution depends on the application: abort, notify the user, or, as here, re-read the item using a new session (the session that received the exception must no longer be used), and repeat the operation. The restocked inventory is 9 in version 1 (line 41), and the sale of the three bicycles results in an inventory of 6 in version 2 (line 50);
    • line 65: an extension function (Chapter 4) that formats an item’s status for display. It is defined within the program, without modifying the entity.

    Two variants:

    • without a version column, Hibernate can check the old values of the columns themselves: with the annotations [@OptimisticLocking(type = OptimisticLockType.DIRTY)] and [@DynamicUpdate] on the entity, the [WHERE] clause of [UPDATE] contains the value read from each modified column ([where id=? and stockActuel=?]). This is useful for an existing database that cannot be modified;
    • pessimistic concurrency remains possible when conflicts are frequent: [session.find(Article::class.java, 1, LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE)] reads the row with a [select ... for update] order, which locks it until the end of the transaction.

    package sqlbrut

import articles.Article
import articles.BaseArticles
import java.math.BigDecimal
import java.sql.Connection

// Native SQL queries: hand-written, passed as-is to SGBD
fun main() {
    BaseArticles.creerSessionFactory().use { sessionFactory ->
         // The table [articles] is recreated with its six items
        BaseArticles.initialiser(sessionFactory)
        sessionFactory.openSession().use { session ->
             // 1 - a hand-written SQL query that returns entities
            println("--- createNativeQuery : des entités")
            val prixMin = BigDecimal.valueOf(200)
            val chers = session
                .createNativeQuery(
                    """
                    select * from articles
                    where prix > :prixMin order by nom""".trimIndent(), Article::class.java
                )
                .setParameter("prixMin", prixMin)
                .resultList
            chers.forEach { println(it) }

             // 2 - a value passed as a parameter: no SQL injection possible
            println("--- tentative d'injection SQL avec un paramètre")
            val nom = "x' or '1'='1"
            var nb = session
                .createNativeQuery("select count(*) from articles where nom = :nom", Long::class.java)
                .setParameter("nom", nom)
                .singleResult
            println("$nb article(s) trouvé(s)")
             // the same query built using a string template: never do this
            println("--- la même tentative avec un gabarit de chaîne")
            val sql = "select count(*) from articles where nom = '$nom'"
            nb = session.createNativeQuery(sql, Long::class.java).singleResult
            println("$nb article(s) trouvé(s)")

             // 3 - results that are not entities
            println("--- createNativeQuery : des valeurs")
            val noms = session
                .createNativeQuery(
                    "select nom from articles where stockActuel < stockMinimum", String::class.java
                )
                .resultList
            println("en rupture : ${noms.joinToString(", ")}")
            val valeur = session
                .createNativeQuery("select sum(prix * stockActuel) from articles", BigDecimal::class.java)
                .singleResult
            println("valeur du stock : %.2f euros".format(valeur))

             // 4 - an update statement
            println("--- createNativeMutationQuery")
            val nbLignes = session.fromTransaction { _ ->
                session
                    .createNativeMutationQuery(
                        """
                        update articles set prix = prix * :coefficient
                        where nom = :nom""".trimIndent()
                    )
                    .setParameter("coefficient", BigDecimal("0.9"))
                    .setParameter("nom", "arc")
                    .executeUpdate()
            }
            println("$nbLignes ligne(s) modifiée(s)")

             // 5 - the session connection, for standard code
            println("--- doWork : la connexion JDBC")
            session.doWork { connexion: Connection ->
                val requete = "select nom, prix from articles where nom = 'arc'"
                connexion.createStatement().use { ordre ->
                    ordre.executeQuery(requete).use { lignes ->
                        while (lignes.next()) {
                            val prix = lignes.getBigDecimal("prix")
                            println("${lignes.getString("nom")} : %.2f euros".format(prix))
                        }
                    }
                }
            }
        }
    }
}

    Comments:

    • Lines 17–24: [createNativeQuery] executes a query (SQL) that returns rows from an entity's table, and the second parameter ([Article::class.java]) instructs Hibernate to materialize them as entities managed by the session. The column names in the result must match those in the model: [select *] is appropriate here. The query is written as a raw string (["""]), from which [trimIndent] removes the common indentation (Chapter 5). It is passed as-is to SGBD (lines 3–6), except that the parameter named [:prixMin] becomes a parameter JDBC ([?]);
    • lines 29–34: an attempt to inject SQL. The value of [nom] is passed as a parameter: it is compared as-is to the [nom] column, and no item matches (line 16);
    • lines 37–38: the same query constructed using a string template (['$nom']). Templates are so convenient in Kotlin that it’s tempting to use them to build a query: this is a serious mistake. The value of [nom] becomes the code SQL, the condition always evaluates to true (line 20), and the query returns six items (line 21): this is a successful SQL injection. As in Chapter 10, a native query must contain only constant text, with values passed as parameters;
    • Lines 43–52: Queries that return single values ([String], [BigDecimal]): The second parameter of [createNativeQuery] is then the type of the value. For multiple columns, you can specify a data class (whose constructor receives the columns in order) or use [Array<Any>::class.java];
    • lines 56–65: [createNativeMutationQuery] prepares an update statement, executed by [executeUpdate], which returns the number of rows modified. It runs within a transaction: the session’s [fromTransaction] method opens it, commits it, and returns the result of the lambda. The lambda receives the transaction as a parameter; since it does not use it, this parameter is named [_];
    • lines 71–77: [doWork] provides access to the session’s JDBC connection ([java.sql.Connection]) for standard JDBC code (Chapter 10): calling a stored procedure, use of a driver feature... It includes the function [use], which closes the order ([Statement]) and the [ResultSet]. The price of the bow has indeed been reduced by 10% (line 40).

    A note on line 71: the type of the lambda parameter ([connexion: Connection]) is explicitly specified here, which is not standard practice in Kotlin. Without it, the compiler rejects the program:

    1
    error: type annotation class 'org.checkerframework.checker.nullness.qual.UnknownKeyFor' of the inferred type is inaccessible. Check the module classpath for missing or conflicting dependencies.

    The Hibernate interface [Work], which the lambda implements, carries type annotations from the Checker Framework library on its parameter type; these annotations are used by Hibernate developers to verify the usage of [null] in their code. This library is not part of Hibernate’s dependencies; therefore, its annotations are unknown to the compiler, which refuses to infer a type that carries them. By specifying the parameter’s type ourselves, we avoid the inference—and the error. This type of issue sometimes arises when using a Java library from Kotlin: the Java code itself ignores these annotations.

    A native query is not portable from one SGBD to another, and Hibernate cannot validate it before execution: it is reserved for cases where HQL is insufficient. HQL, in fact, covers a large part of SQL (joins of all kinds, subqueries, windowing functions, [union]...), and allows you to call a function from SGBD that it does not recognize.

    11.13. Bulk updates, read-only mode, and batches

    Tracking changes comes at a cost: to increase the price of 100 items, you must read all 100 items, modify them one by one, and the session synchronization will send 100 [UPDATE] commands.     package majenmasse

import articles.Article
import articles.BaseArticles
import java.math.BigDecimal

// Batch processing: update/delete commands HQL, read-only, stateless session, and batches
fun main() {
    BaseArticles.creerSessionFactory().use { sessionFactory ->
         // The table [articles] is recreated with its six records
        BaseArticles.initialiser(sessionFactory)
        sessionFactory.openSession().use { session ->
            var transaction = session.beginTransaction()

             // 1 - Update HQL: a single command UPDATE, no entities loaded into memory
            println("--- réapprovisionnement des articles en rupture")
            var nbLignes = session
                .createMutationQuery(
                    """
                    update Article set stockActuel = stockMinimum * 2
                    where stockActuel < stockMinimum""".trimIndent()
                )
                .executeUpdate()
            println("$nbLignes article(s) modifié(s)")

            println("--- hausse de 10 % des prix inférieurs à 150 euros")
            nbLignes = session
                .createMutationQuery("update Article set prix = prix * 1.1 where prix < 150")
                .executeUpdate()
            println("$nbLignes article(s) modifié(s)")

             // 2 - delete HQL: a single command DELETE
            println("--- suppression des articles de plus de 550 euros")
            nbLignes = session
                .createMutationQuery("delete from Article where prix > 550")
                .executeUpdate()
            println("$nbLignes article(s) supprimé(s)")
            transaction.commit()

             // 3 - read-only: read entities are not monitored
            println("--- lecture seule")
            transaction = session.beginTransaction()
            val articles = session
                .createSelectionQuery("from Article order by id", Article::class.java)
                .setReadOnly(true)
                .resultList
            articles.forEach { println(it) }
             // Modifications to a read-only entity are ignored
            articles.first().prix = BigDecimal.ZERO
            println("session modifiée : ${session.isDirty}")
            transaction.commit()

             // 4 - An `update` command (HQL) does not modify entities already loaded by the session
            println("--- update HQL et entités chargées")
            transaction = session.beginTransaction()
            val pompe = session.find(Article::class.java, 2)
            session.createMutationQuery("update Article set prix = 9.5 where id = :id")
                .setParameter("id", pompe.id)
                .executeUpdate()
            println("prix en mémoire : ${pompe.prix}")
            session.refresh(pompe)
            println("prix après refresh : ${pompe.prix}")
            transaction.commit()
        }

         // 5 - a stateless session (StatelessSession) and commands sent in batches
        println("--- StatelessSession et lots de 3 ordres")
        sessionFactory.inStatelessTransaction { session ->
            session.jdbcBatchSize = 3
            val articles = session
                .createSelectionQuery("from Article order by id", Article::class.java)
                .resultList
            for (article in articles) {
                article.stockActuel += 1
                 // Each modification is explicitly requested: entities are not monitored
                session.update(article)
            }
        }
    }
}

    Comments:

    • Lines 17–23: A [update] command written as HQL, prepared by [createMutationQuery], and executed by [executeUpdate]. It becomes a single order SQL [UPDATE] (lines 4–6), executed by SGBD on all affected lines, without any entity being loaded into memory. The new value may depend on the line itself ([stockMinimum * 2]). Such a command is executed within a transaction (lines 2 and 18);
    • lines 27–29: a 10% increase in low prices. The constants for the query HQL ([1.1], [150]) are written directly into the text of the command SQL (lines 10–11);
    • lines 34–36: a [delete] HQL order removes the bow, the only item priced over 550 euros (lines 14–16);
    • lines 43–50: a read-only operation ([setReadOnly(true)]). The entities being read are managed by the session, but the session does not retain their original state or monitor them: this is faster and more memory-efficient for data that is read without being modified (display, calculations). The trade-off is that any modification to such an entity is ignored (line 49): the session has nothing to synchronize ([session.isDirty] is equal to [false], line 29) and [commit] does not send any commands. You can also set an entire session to read-only ([session.isDefaultReadOnly = true]);
    • lines 56–62: a trap. A command like [update] HQL operates directly on the database: it does not modify entities already loaded by the session. The pump managed by the session retains its old price (line 37) until it is read again with [session.refresh(pompe)] (lines 38–42);
    • Lines 68–76: A stateless session ([StatelessSession]), opened here with a transaction via [inStatelessTransaction]. It has no persistence context: no first-level cache, no change tracking, no lazy loading, and no cascades. Each operation is explicitly requested ([insert], [update], [delete], [get]) and executed as is. This is the tool for bulk processing: importing a large file, recalculating all rows in a table;
    • line 69: the SQL commands will be sent to SGBD in batches (see Chapter 10) of three: the JDBC driver transmits three commands in a single exchange with the server. In Kotlin, the [getJdbcBatchSize]/[setJdbcBatchSize] pair is used as a property. The log shows the first three [UPDATE] entries, followed by the execution of the batch (line 58), and concludes with the final batch of two commands (line 63). An application sets the batch size for all its sessions using the [hibernate.jdbc.batch_size] property (typically between 10 and 50). Note that inserts into a table whose key is generated by [IDENTITY] cannot be grouped into batches.

    For bulk processing with a regular session, you must prevent its persistence context from accumulating entities: synchronize and flush the session regularly, for example every fifty records ([session.flush(); session.clear()]). With Kotlin, the [chunked] function for sequences and collections (Chapter 5) conveniently splits the data into chunks of this size.

    11.14. Hibernate and Dependency Injection: Spring

    11.14.1. The [SessionFactory] in the container

    The previous examples created their own sessions. In a layered application (Chapter 6), and in all Spring applications, the [SessionFactory] is an object in the dependency injection container, just like the layers that use it. To this end, the Spring Framework provides, in its [spring-orm] library:

    • the [LocalSessionFactoryBean] class, which constructs the [SessionFactory] from a data source ([DataSource], Chapter 10) and a list of entities;
    • the [HibernateTransactionManager] class, a transaction manager that opens a Hibernate session for each transaction, associates it with the current thread, and closes it at the end of the transaction;
    • the [@Transactional] annotation (library [spring-tx]): when applied to a method, or to a class for all its public methods, it instructs Spring to execute the method within a transaction, which is committed if the method completes normally and rolled back if it throws an uncaught exception. These are known as declarative transactions. A note regarding Kotlin: by default, Spring does not roll back the transaction for a controlled exception as defined by Java (a [IOException], for example). Kotlin does not distinguish these exceptions from others, but Spring does: a Kotlin function that throws a [IOException] within a transactional method will have its transaction committed! We therefore write [@Transactional(rollbackFor = [Exception::class])] to ensure the transaction is rolled back in all cases.

    Inside a transactional method, ***[sessionFactory.currentSession]*** (the *[getCurrentSession] method) resets the current transaction session. A [dao] layer can then be a singleton that receives the [SessionFactory] (thread-safe) and asks it, in each method, for the current session: the rule “one session per unit of work, never shared between threads” is effortlessly enforced. Be careful with coroutines, however: the current session is associated with the thread, and a suspension function that switches threads in the middle of a transaction would lose its session. Therefore, we retain the blocking transactional methods and call them from a coroutine within a [withContext(Dispatchers.IO)] block, as shown in the example [asynchrone]*.

    package injection

import articles.Article
import articles.BaseArticles
import com.zaxxer.hikari.HikariDataSource
import java.util.Properties
import javax.sql.DataSource
import org.hibernate.SessionFactory
import org.hibernate.cfg.AvailableSettings
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration
import org.springframework.orm.jpa.hibernate.HibernateTransactionManager
import org.springframework.orm.jpa.hibernate.LocalSessionFactoryBean
import org.springframework.transaction.annotation.EnableTransactionManagement

// the Spring configuration: connection pool, SessionFactory, transaction manager, [dao] layer
@Configuration
@EnableTransactionManagement
class Config {

     // the connection pool HikariCP (Chapter 10)
    @Bean(destroyMethod = "close")
    fun dataSource() = HikariDataSource().apply {
        jdbcUrl = BaseArticles.URL
        username = BaseArticles.UTILISATEUR
        password = BaseArticles.MOT_DE_PASSE
    }

     // the SessionFactory, created by Spring using the connection pool
    @Bean
    fun sessionFactory(dataSource: DataSource) = LocalSessionFactoryBean().apply {
        setDataSource(dataSource)
        setAnnotatedClasses(Article::class.java)
        hibernateProperties = Properties().apply { put(AvailableSettings.FORMAT_SQL, "true") }
    }

     // the transaction manager: one Hibernate session per transaction
    @Bean
    fun transactionManager(sessionFactory: SessionFactory) = HibernateTransactionManager(sessionFactory)

     // the [dao] layer: a singleton that receives the SessionFactory
    @Bean
    fun articlesDao(sessionFactory: SessionFactory) = ArticlesDao(sessionFactory)
}
    • line 18: enables the [@Transactional] annotation: Spring will replace every object with a method bearing this annotation with a proxy that opens and commits the transaction around the call;
    • lines 22–26: the HikariCP connection pool from Chapter 10, configured in a [apply] block: The modifiers [setJdbcUrl], [setUsername], and [setPassword] are used as properties. The attribute [destroyMethod] specifies the method to be called when the container is shut down. The inferred return type of the function is [HikariDataSource]: this is the type under which Spring registers the bean;
    • lines 31–34: [SessionFactory]. A *[LocalSessionFactoryBean] is a factory for *[SessionFactory]*: Spring registers the object it produces in the container, and it is a *[SessionFactory] that is obtained by requesting this bean. It receives the connection pool (which replaces Hibernate’s built-in pool), the entities, and the Hibernate properties. We write [setDataSource(dataSource)] rather than [dataSource = dataSource], which would assign the parameter to itself (and would be rejected, since a parameter is read-only);
    • line 39: the transaction manager;
    • line 43: the [dao] layer, which receives the [SessionFactory].

    package injection

import articles.Article
import org.hibernate.Session
import org.hibernate.SessionFactory
import org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Transactional

// the [dao] layer: each public method runs within a transaction opened by Spring
@Transactional
class ArticlesDao(
     // the SessionFactory, shared by all threads
    private val sessionFactory: SessionFactory
) {

     // Do two requests from the current session, within the same transaction, refer to the same session?
    fun memeSession() = sessionFactory.currentSession === sessionFactory.currentSession

     // the transaction session
    fun session(): Session = sessionFactory.currentSession

     // the items to be restocked; a read-only transaction
    @Transactional(readOnly = true)
    fun articlesEnRupture(): List<String> {
        val hql = "select nom from Article where stockActuel < stockMinimum"
        return sessionFactory.currentSession.createSelectionQuery(hql, String::class.java).resultList
    }

     // the item with the given name
    @Transactional(readOnly = true)
    fun article(nom: String): Article =
        sessionFactory.currentSession
            .createSelectionQuery("from Article where nom = :nom", Article::class.java)
            .setParameter("nom", nom)
            .singleResult

     // the sale of a quantity of an item: an exception rolls back the transaction
    fun vendre(nom: String, quantite: Int) {
        val article = article(nom)
        article.stockActuel -= quantite
         // check triggers a IllegalStateException if the condition is false
        check(article.stockActuel >= 0) { "stock insuffisant pour l'article [$nom]" }
    }
}
    • line 9: all public methods of the class are transactional;
    • line 12: the [SessionFactory], received by the primary constructor;
    • line 16: within the same transaction, do two requests from the current session return the same session? The [===] operator compares the references (Chapter 3);
    • line 19: the transaction’s session, returned to the caller (for the following experiment: this is not done in a real application);
    • lines 22–25: a read-only transaction ([readOnly = true]): Spring sets the session to read-only and does not synchronize it;
    • lines 37–41: the sale of a quantity of an item. If the inventory becomes negative, the Kotlin function [check] (Chapter 3) throws a [IllegalStateException], an unhandled exception: Spring rolls back the transaction. The call to the [article] method (line 38) is an internal call within the object, which does not go through the proxy: it executes within the [vendre] transaction.

    The proxy created by Spring for the [ArticlesDao] class is a subclass of it, generated at runtime by the CGLIB library, which redefines each public method to wrap it in a transaction. Without the [plugin.spring] plugin, the Kotlin class would be final, and Spring would not be able to derive from it. If you compile the subproject without this plugin (by manually declaring the [Config] class and its [open] functions to work around the first error, which we already encountered in Chapter 6), the container refuses to start:

    1
2
3
    Exception in thread "main" org.springframework.beans.factory.BeanCreationException: Error creating bean with name 'articlesDao' defined in injection.Config: Could not generate CGLIB subclass of class injection.ArticlesDao: Common causes of this problem include using a final class or a non-visible class
Caused by: org.springframework.aop.framework.AopConfigException: Could not generate CGLIB subclass of class injection.ArticlesDao: Common causes of this problem include using a final class or a non-visible class
Caused by: java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: Cannot subclass final class injection.ArticlesDao

    A more insidious pitfall awaits anyone who manually opens the class ([open class ArticlesDao]) without opening its methods: the proxy is then created, but it cannot override the methods that remain final. Calling these methods directly executes the code of the [ArticlesDao]... class on the proxy object, whose fields have not been initialized (Spring creates it without calling the class’s constructor). The result, obtained by compiling the subproject in this way, is confusing:

    1
2
    --- sessions et transactions
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.NullPointerException: Cannot invoke "org.hibernate.SessionFactory.getCurrentSession()" because "this.sessionFactory" is null

    The property [sessionFactory], which is of a non-nullable type, is set to [null]! The plugin prevents these two errors: with it, the class and all its methods are open.

    package injection

import articles.BaseArticles
import org.hibernate.HibernateException
import org.hibernate.SessionFactory
import org.springframework.beans.factory.getBean
import org.springframework.context.annotation.AnnotationConfigApplicationContext

// Hibernate in the Spring container: current session and declarative transactions
fun main() {
     // the Spring container, configured by the class [Config]
    AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(Config::class.java).use { contexte ->
         // The table [articles] is recreated with its six records
        val sessionFactory = contexte.getBean<SessionFactory>()
        BaseArticles.initialiser(sessionFactory)
        val dao = contexte.getBean<ArticlesDao>()

         // 1 - During a transaction, the current session remains the same
        println("--- sessions et transactions")
        println("une transaction : même session = ${dao.memeSession()}")
         // 2 - Two transactions: two sessions, closed at the end of their respective transactions
        val session1 = dao.session()
        val session2 = dao.session()
        println("deux transactions : même session = ${session1 === session2}, " +
                "première session ouverte = ${session1.isOpen}")
         // 3 - Outside of a transaction, there is no current session
        try {
            sessionFactory.currentSession
        } catch (e: HibernateException) {
            println("${e::class.simpleName} : ${e.message}")
        }

         // 4 - transactional methods of the [dao] layer
        println("--- articles en rupture")
        println("en rupture : ${dao.articlesEnRupture()}")
        println("--- vente de 2 vélos")
        dao.vendre("vélo", 2)
        println("--- vente de 50 pompes")
        try {
            dao.vendre("pompe", 50)
        } catch (e: IllegalStateException) {
            println("${e::class.simpleName} : ${e.message}")
        }
        println("--- état de la base")
        println(dao.article("vélo"))
        println(dao.article("pompe"))
    }
}

    Comments:

    • Line 12: the Spring container, configured by the [Config] class. It is closed at the end of the [use] block, which closes the [SessionFactory] and the connection pool;
    • line 14: the [SessionFactory] constructed by Spring, obtained via Spring’s [getBean<T>()] extension function (Chapter 6); it is used to recreate the product table;
    • line 20: a transaction (lines 3–4): within the same transaction, the current session remains the same (line 5);
    • lines 22–25: two calls, two transactions (lines 6–9), two different sessions; the first is closed, since its transaction is complete (line 10). The property [isOpen] is the session’s method [isOpen()];
    • lines 28–29: outside a transaction, there is no current session: [getCurrentSession] launches a [HibernateException] (line 11). This is the classic error of a method that omitted the annotation [@Transactional];
    • line 35: a read-only transaction (lines 13–17);
    • line 37: the sale of two bicycles. The transaction is committed, and session synchronization sends the [UPDATE] (lines 20–33);
    • lines 40–41: the sale of fifty pumps triggers an exception: Spring rolls back the transaction (line 40), and [UPDATE] is never sent, since the session was not synchronized;
    • lines 45–46: database state: the bicycle inventory has changed to 8, while the pump inventory remains at 10 (lines 49 and 56).

    In a Spring Boot application, all of this happens automatically: Spring Boot creates the connection pool, the factory (in its Jakarta Persistence form, a [EntityManagerFactory]), and the transaction manager from the [application.properties] file. Spring Data JPA is often used on top of Hibernate; it generates the [dao] layer from a simple interface: [interface ArticleRepository : JpaRepository<Article, Int>] provides [findAll], [findById], [save], [delete]..., and a declared method [fun findByPrixLessThan(prix: BigDecimal): List<Article>] is automatically translated into a query. Spring Data adds a few extension functions for Kotlin, such as [findByIdOrNull], which returns a [Article?] rather than a [Optional<Article>].

    11.15. Sample Application - Version 7

    11.15.1. The Architecture

    Version 6 of the tax calculation application (Chapter 10) read the tax brackets from a MySQL database using JDBC. Version 7 does the same using Hibernate. As with version 6, only the [dao] layer changes: the [metier] and [ui] layers from version 5 (Chapter 6) are reused as-is, thanks to the composite architecture.

@Entity
@Table(name = "tranches")
class Tranche(
    @Column(name = "limite", nullable = false, precision = 10, scale = 2)
    private var limite: BigDecimal,

    @Column(name = "coeffr", nullable = false, precision = 6, scale = 4)
    private var coeffR: BigDecimal,

    @Column(name = "coeffn", nullable = false, precision = 10, scale = 2)
    private var coeffN: BigDecimal,
) {
     // the primary key, which does not exist in the TrancheImpot class
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private var id: Int? = null
}

The column names are in lowercase. The properties are private: the entity is used only to populate the table ([CreationBase]) and to write queries; the rest of the application never sees it. Hibernate, which accesses the fields directly, does not require them to be public;

    package impots.dao

import impots.entites.ImpotException
import impots.entites.TrancheImpot
import jakarta.persistence.PersistenceException
import org.hibernate.jpa.HibernatePersistenceConfiguration

// a layer [dao] that reads tax brackets from a database using Hibernate
class HibernateImpot(url: String, utilisateur: String, motDePasse: String) : IImpotDao {

    companion object {
         // error codes specific to this implementation
        const val ERREUR_ACCES = 1
        const val TABLE_VIDE = 2
    }

     // tax brackets, loaded once and for all during initialization
    override val tranchesImpot: List<TrancheImpot> = try {
         // a short-lived SessionFactory, lasting only long enough to read the table
        HibernatePersistenceConfiguration("impots")
            .managedClass(Tranche::class.java)
            .jdbcUrl(url)
            .jdbcCredentials(utilisateur, motDePasse)
            .createEntityManagerFactory()
            .use { sessionFactory ->
                 // The table rows are projected onto the application’s TrancheImpot class
                val hql = "select limite, coeffR, coeffN from Tranche order by id"
                sessionFactory.fromSession { session ->
                    session.createSelectionQuery(hql, TrancheImpot::class.java).resultList
                }
            }
    } catch (e: PersistenceException) {
         // Hibernate or SGBD error: it is encapsulated in a ImpotException
        throw ImpotException("Erreur lors de la lecture des tranches d'impôt dans la base de données",
            e, ERREUR_ACCES)
    }

    init {
         // The [metier] layer requires at least one slice
        if (tranchesImpot.isEmpty()) {
            throw ImpotException("La table des tranches d'impôt est vide", code = TABLE_VIDE)
        }
    }
}
    • lines 11–14: the error codes for this implementation, as with [FileImpot] and [JsonImpot];
    • line 9: the [dao] layer receives the URL from the database, along with the user and their password. These are simply constructor parameters ([val] is not written: they do not become properties, since they are used only for construction). It reads the slices once and for all during construction: it will be a singleton;
    • line 18: the property [tranchesImpot] of the interface [IImpotDao], initialized by an expression [try] (Chapter 3): its value is that of the block [try]; if an error occurs, [catch] throws an exception;
    • Lines 20–25: A short-lived [SessionFactory]—just long enough to read the table—immediately closed by [use]. Since the layer accesses the database only once, there is no need to keep it; a [dao] layer that accessed the database on every call would instead receive a [SessionFactory] created once and for all, as in the previous example;
    • Lines 27–29: Reading the table in primary key order. The query is a projection onto the data class [TrancheImpot]: Hibernate requests only the three relevant columns from SGBD and directly creates the application objects by calling the constructor of *[TrancheImpot] with the three values, without going through *[Tranche] entities. The value returned by [fromSession], and then by [use], is the list that was read: this is the value of the property;
    • Lines 32–35: An error from Hibernate or SGBD (database inaccessible, table missing, etc.) manifests as a [PersistenceException] (the base class for Jakarta Persistence exceptions, from which Hibernate’s exceptions are derived). As in other implementations, it is encapsulated within a *[ImpotException]. The exception can occur as early as the creation of the *[SessionFactory]* (line 24), which connects to the server: it is also contained within the ***[try]** block;
    • lines 38–41: an empty table is also an error: the [metier] layer requires at least one row. The [init] block executes after the property is initialized, which precedes it in the class. The error code is passed via a named argument ([code = TABLE_VIDE]), since the exception has no cause (Chapter 6).

    package impots.dao

import org.hibernate.jpa.HibernatePersistenceConfiguration
import org.hibernate.tool.schema.Action

// creation of the database [hbimpots]: the table [tranches], populated with the slices from HardwiredImpot
fun main() {
    HibernatePersistenceConfiguration("impots")
        .managedClass(Tranche::class.java)
        .jdbcUrl("jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/hbimpots?createDatabaseIfNotExist=true")
        .jdbcCredentials("root", "")
         // display of orders SQL, without formatting
        .showSql(true, false, false)
         // the table is deleted and then recreated when SessionFactory is created
        .schemaToolingAction(Action.CREATE)
        .createEntityManagerFactory()
        .use { sessionFactory ->
             // the pay scale brackets from version 5, numbered starting at 1 by SGBD
            sessionFactory.inTransaction { session ->
                for ((limite, coeffR, coeffN) in HardwiredImpot().tranchesImpot) {
                    session.persist(Tranche(limite, coeffR, coeffN))
                }
            }
        }
}
    • line 10: the database [hbimpots], created by MySQL if it does not exist;
    • line 13: displays the SQL orders, without formatting;
    • line 15: the table is deleted and then recreated when [SessionFactory] is created;
    • lines 19–21: one [Tranche] entity per slice of the [HardwiredImpot] class, persisted in a transaction. The [for] loop breaks down each [TrancheImpot] into its three components ([(limite, coeffR, coeffN)]) using the functions [component1], [component2], and [component3], which are generated for a data class (Chapter 4).

    <?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!-- Logback configuration: only Hibernate errors are displayed -->
<configuration>
    <appender name="CONSOLE" class="ch.qos.logback.core.ConsoleAppender">
        <encoder>
            <pattern>%-5level %logger{0} - %msg%n</pattern>
        </encoder>
    </appender>
     <!-- Errors from SGBD are passed to the application as exceptions: they are not logged -->
    <logger name="org.hibernate.orm.jdbc.error" level="OFF"/>
    <root level="ERROR">
        <appender-ref ref="CONSOLE"/>
    </root>
</configuration>
    • line 10: Errors from SGBD, which Hibernate logs before throwing an exception, are not displayed: the application reports them itself;
    • Line 11: The other logs record only errors.

    To create the database on your own system:

    • run MySQL (in Laragon; see the appendix; user [root] with no password);
    • navigate to the [11-hibernate] folder and enter the command [gradlew -q :ImpotsV7:impots-dao-hibernate:run] (or run [CreationBase.kt] in IntelliJ IDEA, with the green triangle placed in front of its function [main]).     The database [hbimpots] is then created, with its table [tranches] populated. If the command fails, verify that MySQL is running and that the URL for [CreationBase.kt] corresponds to your server (port 3306, username [root], empty password). Alternatively, if you prefer, you can create the table and its rows using a SQL script, as described in Chapter 10.

import java.util.Properties
import kotlin.io.path.Path
import kotlin.io.path.bufferedReader
import kotlin.system.exitProcess
import org.springframework.beans.factory.getBean
import org.springframework.context.support.GenericApplicationContext
import org.springframework.context.support.registerBean

// Version 7: The [dao] layer reads tax brackets from a database using Hibernate
fun main(args: Array<String>) {
     // the configuration file: impots-hibernate.properties by default, or the one passed as an argument
    val fichierConfig = args.firstOrNull() ?: "impots-hibernate.properties"

     // integration of layers
    val metier: IImpotMetier = try {
         // Reading the configuration from the current directory
        val config = Properties()
        Path(fichierConfig).bufferedReader().use { config.load(it) }
        val url = config.getProperty("jdbc.url")
            ?: throw ImpotException("URL [jdbc.url] de la base absente du fichier $fichierConfig")
        val utilisateur = config.getProperty("jdbc.utilisateur", "root")
        val motDePasse = config.getProperty("jdbc.motdepasse", "")

         // the Spring container: layers are registered here
        val contexte = GenericApplicationContext()
         // the layer [dao]: HibernateImpot, with the configuration base
        contexte.registerBean<IImpotDao> { HibernateImpot(url, utilisateur, motDePasse) }
         // the [metier] layer from version 5: the container will pass it the [dao] layer
        contexte.registerBean<ImpotMetier>()

         // container startup: it creates the [dao] layer, then the [metier] layer
        contexte.refresh()
        contexte.getBean<IImpotMetier>()
    } catch (e: Exception) {
         // Displays the error and stops the program
        Dialogue.afficherErreur(e)
        exitProcess(1)
    }

     // user dialog, the one from version 5
    Dialogue.run(metier)
}
    • The file is not named [Main.kt]: it would be compiled into a class named [impots.ui.MainKt], which already exists in the [impots-ui] module of version 5, on which we depend. The file [MainHibernate.kt] generates a class named [impots.ui.MainHibernateKt];
    • lines 26–29: the required URL database, the username, and the password, read from the configuration. [getProperty] returns [null] for a missing key: the Elvis operator ([?:]) then evaluates to [ImpotException] ([throw] is a Kotlin expression);
    • line 34: the [dao] layer is a [HibernateImpot], created by a lambda that passes it the parameters from the base;
    • line 36: the [metier] layer in version 5: the container will pass the [dao] layer to its constructor;
    • line 48: the dialog for version 5.

    • line 12: the original exception, thrown by the JDBC driver;
    • lines 8 and 10: the Hibernate exceptions that encapsulate it: the error occurred during the creation of [SessionFactory], when Hibernate connected to the server to determine its version;
    • line 6: the [dao] layer wrapped the error in a [ImpotException];
    • line 4: the Spring container, which was creating the [dao] layer, itself encapsulated the exception in a [BeanCreationException], which was displayed by the main program.

    Changing SGBD is equivalent to changing the URL in the database and the dependency on the JDBC driver: Hibernate automatically selects the SQL dialect from the encountered SGBD, and the code for the [HibernateImpot] class, written in HQL, remains unchanged. Only the database creation—which depends on the column types—needs to be redone, which the program [CreationBase.kt] does without any modifications other than to its own URL.

    11.16. Conclusion: JDBC, JdbcClient, jOOQ—Exposed or Hibernate?

    We now have two ways to access a database: JDBC (Chapter 10) and Hibernate (this chapter). There are other, intermediate approaches that are widely used:

    • JdbcClient, from the Spring Framework ([spring-jdbc] library), adds to JDBC a flexible API that executes a hand-written SQL query and automatically transforms the result rows into objects: [jdbcClient.sql("select * from articles where prix > :prix").param("prix", 200).query(Article::class.java).list()]. You write the SQL; Spring handles the parameters and copies the columns into the objects (including data classes, whose constructors receive the columns). This is a “micro-ORM”;
    • jOOQ generates, from the database schema, classes that allow you to write a SQL in Java or Kotlin that is verified by the compiler: [dsl.selectFrom(ARTICLES).where(ARTICLES.PRIX.gt(prix)).fetch()]. You retain full control over the SQL, with the safety of type checking;
    • Exposed, from JetBrains, is the database access library written in Kotlin and for Kotlin. Tables are described there using Kotlin objects ([object Articles : Table("articles")], with columns such as [val prix = decimal("prix", 10, 2)]), without code generation, and queries are written in a dedicated language (“ DSL”), which resembles SQL and is verified by the compiler: [Articles.selectAll().where { Articles.prix greater prixMin }]. Exposed also offers a second API, a lightweight version of ORM (entity classes linked to tables), and relies on JDBC or, optionally, on non-blocking drivers (R2DBC) that can be used from coroutines. It takes advantage of everything we’ve covered about Kotlin: extension functions, lambdas with receivers, infix functions ([greater]), and nullable types for optional columns.
     
    Strengths
    Weaknesses
    JDBC
    Full control over SQL; performance; no dependencies
    a lot of repetitive code (parameters, reading columns), streamlined in Kotlin by [use] and extension functions; SQL in strings, not checked by the compiler
    JdbcClient
    SQL hand-written, without copy-and-paste code; performance similar to JDBC
    No change tracking or generation of [INSERT]/[UPDATE]; SQL not verified
    jOOQ
    SQL verified by the compiler; all features of SGBD
    Code generation with every schema change; no change tracking; paid license required for certain commercial SGBD versions
    Exposed
    Designed for Kotlin; queries verified by the compiler, without code generation; lightweight
    Kotlin-specific; less widespread than Hibernate, and less documentation; the schema is described manually in the code
    Hibernate
    object-oriented model; change tracking; relationships; HQL and API Criteria; Jakarta Persistence standard; independent of the SGBD
    an additional layer to understand (sessions, states, lazy loading); SQL generated code to monitor; less suitable for complex bulk processing; some adaptations for Kotlin ([jpa] and [allopen] plugins, no data classes for entities)

    The following guidelines can be suggested:

    • Hibernate (often via Spring Data JPA) is suitable for most business applications: a model of interconnected entities, operations for reading and updating entities, and a schema that evolves with the application. It is the default choice for Spring Boot applications, in both Kotlin and Java;
    • JDBC, JdbcClient, jOOQ or Exposed are suitable when you want precise control over the SQL being executed: complex statistical queries, stored procedures, processing very large volumes, or an existing database with a schema that is poorly suited to an object-oriented model. Exposed is a natural choice for an application written entirely in Kotlin, particularly outside of Spring (using the Ktor web framework from JetBrains, for example);
    • these approaches can be combined: an application can use Hibernate for the bulk of its operations and hand-written SQL code—in the form of native queries—with [JdbcClient] or JDBC ([doWork]), for a few critical queries.

    In any case, ORM does not eliminate the need to understand SQL and how SGBD works: the log of executed SQL commands, which we have displayed throughout this chapter, is the primary tool for verifying what Hibernate is actually doing.

    To learn more, the Hibernate documentation is comprehensive, and its introductory guide is the best place to start: Hibernate ORM - documentation. The Jakarta Persistence specification is published by the Eclipse Foundation: Jakarta Persistence. Spring’s guide on using JPA in Kotlin summarizes the concepts covered in this chapter (plugs, entities, nullability): Building web applications with Spring Boot and Kotlin. Exposed is presented on its GitHub page, which links to its documentation: JetBrains Exposed.
